articles.title: Manchester City staff invited on government trade trip to India
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Greater Manchester mayor Bev Craig invited City representative on trade trip organised by business secretary

A club representative from Manchester City was invited on a…

blocks.text: A club representative from Manchester City was invited on a government-backed trade delegation to India this week, despite the club being found guilty of 114 breaches of Premier League rules.

Andy Burnham’s successor as Manchester mayor Bev Craig took a representative from the club to Delhi and Mumbai on a trip organised by business secretary Jonathan Reynolds, where she and other northern mayors have been promoting British trade and tourism.

She defended the decision to invite City even as the prime minister came under fire for his own contacts with the club, telling the Guardian it had played a vital role in helping build infrastructure in her city.
“If a football club has broken the rules, a football club should be punished for breaking the rules, and that is pretty clear in an independent process,” she said.

“I think what can also be true at the same time though, if you ask residents in east Manchester, have they benefited from a new library, a new leisure centre, a new sixth-form college, infrastructure investment, the job opportunities that come from them being a good employment charter signee and an early adopter of the real living wage – then they will have felt that benefit.”
City, which says it is innocent of the charges and has appealed against them, declined to comment.

The revelation comes as Burnham faced pressure over his relationship with City’s owners during his time as mayor of Greater Manchester. The prime minister was forced to clarify on Wednesday that he had two additional dinners with the club chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, at the Etihad Stadium, having previously declared those only as matchday hospitality.
Speaking at PMQs, Burnham said no one from the club had raised the Premier League charges with him.
Craig’s defence of the club came as her mayoral authority published details of Burnham’s contacts with City officials when he was mayor.

The release showed the prime minister had attended a formal meeting with al-Mubarak, chatted to him in the stands at a player’s testimonial game and was accompanied by staff from the club on official overseas visits.

But the Sun newspaper revealed later on Monday that Burnham had twice attended a pre-match dinner with the chair, which was declared in now-deleted council paperwork. No 10 said it was routine for the records to be deleted when a new mayor was in place.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham with Khaldoon al-Mubarak.  Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

blocks.text: Burnham’s initial response to the findings against City had drawn criticism after he said he would be “really concerned” if its Abu Dhabi owners sold the club in the wake of the Premier League findings, calling them a “huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”.
As the prime minister came under fire for his comments, Downing Street clarified that he believed where wrongdoing had been established, those responsible should face the consequences.

City attended the trade delegation alongside several other northern sports and leisure organisations, including Lancashire cricket club and Visit Lake District. While in India, the football club took part in an event in Delhi promoting British tourism.
The Great North – a coalition of mayors from the north of England which organised the India event – said its aim was “to shine a spotlight on the great tourism products across the north of England”.​
after newsletter promotion

The Greater Manchester mayoral authority said on Tuesday that representatives of Greater Manchester sporting clubs would “routinely join business delegations” on international visits during Burnham’s time as mayor.

Burnham’s defence of City and its owners has focused attention not only on his links to the club but on how reliant he was on investment from Abu Dhabi to power Manchester’s strong growth rates when he was mayor.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham with Bev Craig after her victory in the Greater Manchester mayoral election. Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA

blocks.text: Other senior politicians on this week’s trade delegation include Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, Douglas Alexander, the Scotland secretary, and Angela Eagle, the environment secretary.

Reynolds took part in a Premier League event on Tuesday, where he met schoolchildren being taught by British-trained coaches. He denied afterwards that the charges against City had tainted the league’s reputation. It is otherwise one of Britain’s most successful cultural exports.
“The brand of the Premier League – one of the UK’s most important brands … that is incredibly powerful,” he said.

Asked whether it was appropriate for City to have been invited, given the charges it faced, he said: “That’s a Greater Manchester issue, and obviously they are a major participant in the economy in Greater Manchester.
“I understand the interest – the relationship between Manchester and Manchester City – but in terms of the allegations, their appeal, that is a football matter.”

articles.title: The Archers cast ‘angry’ at BBC decision to scrap new studio, says actor
articles.summary:
Ben Norris says cost-cutting measure that means show will be recorded outside Birmingham risks ‘extraordinary burden’ for crew

A cast member of The Archers has said its actors have been…

blocks.text: A cast member of The Archers has said its actors have been angered by the BBC’s decision to axe the show’s new studio, in a move that could lead to it being recorded away from its home in Birmingham.
Ben Norris, who plays Ben Archer in the world’s longest-running soap opera, said the decision risked having a real impact on the quality of the show and placing an “extraordinary burden” on its crew.

Norris told the Guardian that current plans, which would involve production staff working in a separate location to the actors recording the show, represented “classic short-termism and doesn’t represent value for money for the licence fee payer”.

“This isn’t us actors being averse to change,” he said. “It’s very much us wanting to stand in solidarity with our colleagues in production, us wanting to ensure the continued highest quality of the programme for the listeners, the continued heritage of the show, its connection to Birmingham, and also for the BBC not to go back on many promises it made to the region.

blocks.caption: Ben Norris, who plays Ben Archer in the BBC Radio 4 drama. Photograph: Steve Ullathorne

blocks.text: “It’s a combination of all those things that has left us feeling as angry as we are.”

Staff were informed last week that the BBC, as part of its £500m cost-cutting drive, had ditched plans for a new radio drama theatre at the Tea Factory in Digbeth, the corporation’s new Birmingham headquarters.
While production staff will still move to the facility, the broadcaster is now looking for an existing UK studio where the show could be recorded.
The West Midlands is included in the search, but there is no guarantee The Archers will be recorded in the region in which it has been based since its launch 75 years ago.
Cast members met on Monday to discuss the announcement. Norris said there were practical problems with the new plan, including the need for last-minute script discussions and specific facilities.

“The Archers is recorded in a very specific way that is unlike almost all other audio drama,” he said. “There are very few other studios that have those facilities, and none that are up to the same specifications as our current setup.
“[The current studio setup] would need transporting, building and striking with any new space we travel to, placing an extraordinary burden on the technical team and incurring extra financial drain.

“I also think it’s a totally false economy. I’ve been told that the additional cost of shipping those people to wherever we ended up would cancel out what it costs to build the new studio within five years, so it’s classic short-termism and doesn’t represent value for money for the licence fee payer at all.”
He said that while actors were based in different places, there was a “big Midlands connection within the cast – either people who grew up or trained there or people who live there now”.
after newsletter promotion

“For day players, of which the Archers has many – coming in to play somebody’s midwife, somebody’s mechanic – those roles often go to local actors and should go to local actors because it’s one of the places that people can start their careers,” he said. “It’s the same for the writing team and the production team.

“This decision flies completely in the face of the BBC and the government’s commitment to pursue as much regionality as possible and to have culture and the economy thriving in every postcode across the UK.”
Norris feared listeners would eventually notice the impact.

“We’re worried about the sustainability of this way of working,” he said. “We are worried about the relationship between cast and crew, but also their energy levels, their wellbeing … Maybe we’d get away with it for a bit, but we think at some point the show would suffer and the listeners would perceive that.”
The performing arts union Equity has said it will oppose the BBC’s plans.

Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, said hemet the West Midlands mayor, Richard Parker, on Wednesday to explore opportunities to continue to record the show in the region once it left Birmingham.

articles.title: Plan unveiled to increase share of land farmed organically in England to 10%
articles.summary:
Government says ambition for 2036 will be good for food and climate resilience, but concerns remain over funding

The government has set an ambition to increase the share of English land…

blocks.text: The government has set an ambition to increase the share of English land farmed organically to 10% by 2036, but concerns remain over how the transition will be funded.

Currently, just 3.4% of England’s agricultural land is farmed organically, one of the smallest shares in Europe. France, for example, farms 10.4% of its land organically, and aims to increase this to 18% by 2027.

Rob Haward, the chief executive of organic veg box company Riverford, said it was a reflection of organic farming having political backing in the EU. Whereas in England, the last organic farming plan was published more than two decades ago.

The government’s new plan, which has been more than three years in the making, sets out a vision for growth in the organic sector, with public procurement – in schools and hospitals, for example – cited as a significant opportunity. The government already has a long-term ambition for 10% of public sector food spend to meet higher environmental production standards. The plan states that the organic sector can play a vital role in achieving this.

The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, said the plan was about “opening up opportunities across the sector, from backing farmers already producing organic food to helping others decide whether it could work for their businesses”.
She added: “Organic farming should not be treated as a niche. More people are looking closely at where their food comes from, how it is produced and whether it meets standards they value.”

Haward said public procurement was “impenetrable” for small organic farms, but hoped the plan would be a “catalyst for growth”. However, he said the sector now needed proper backing from the government, including grant funding.

In September, thousands of farmers were left empty-handed after the government’s sustainable farming incentive 2026 (SFI) funding was spent in just six hours. This meant that some farmers who might have been planning to use the funding to transition to organic farming may have missed out.
“SFI needs to be reliable, successful and secure to enable this transition,” said Haward. “It’s hard for any farm to invest in their business if things change, we need some consistency.”
Gareth Morgan, the head of farming policy at the Soil Association, said there had been a lot of discussions with Defra about funding, but in the end “there has been a compromise”.
“There is now an urgent need to reopen SFI to enable farms to move to organic farming,” he said.

Morgan added that increasing the share of land farmed organically could bring down the price of organic food for consumers. “Currently the price of food is subsidised and we don’t pay for the environmental impact. If organic food becomes more mainstream, the price difference will become less,” he said.

Martin Lines, the chief executive of the Nature Friendly Farming Network, said farmers could not rely on government funding alone to make this transition, and said there needs to be “real investment from the supply chain and the private sector, along with fairer prices for farmers for their goods and stronger domestic markets for homegrown produce”.
The National Farmers’ Union, whose members include organic and non-organic farms, said the plan signified a “really positive step forward … for the wider supply chain”.

“Supporting domestic production will strengthen the resilience of our food supply chains and ensure British farmers and growers benefit from opportunities, rather than increasing our reliance on imports,” said Paul Tompkins, the deputy president of the union.

In the plan’s foreword, Eagle said: “Across England, organic farmers, growers and food businesses play an important role in producing high-quality food while caring for soils, wildlife and the rural communities they are part of. In doing so, they also help advance wider goals for nature recovery, cleaner water and greater climate resilience.”

This year has been challenging for farmers because of crop-destroying heat and drought alongside soaring fertiliser costs tied to the war in Iran. Organic farms have been found to be more resilient in the face of these extreme weather conditions and are also not affected by rising fertiliser costs.
“Organic farmers are much less exposed to these risks,” Morgan said, adding that the plan was a sign that the government was thinking hard about the pathway for food security.

articles.title: Netflix to lay off 1,000 staff in steepest cuts since 2022
articles.summary: The cuts equate to around 6% of the streaming giant's total workforce worldwide.

blocks.text: Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals.
The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce.
Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to".

The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers.

In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation".
Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount.

Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources."
Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon".
The email added that the firm was on track to meet its financial forecasts. The streaming service is due to report its latest results on 20 October.
Investors have been weighing up user engagement - the amount of time customers spend on Netflix - as it competes with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok.
The firm has continued to commission shows - its most popular at the moment is "Below", an underwater mystery series.
It has also been attempting to expand its business, including gaming and allowing adverts to play before and during shows and films.
However, "they haven't been able to find another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer.
He added that the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a plateau.
"Eventually, because they're nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle," he said.
The last major redundancy round at Netflix was in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade.

articles.title: Joni Mitchell becomes a U.S. citizen, 'a journey that began 62 years ago'
articles.summary: More than six decades after leaving Canada, legendary singer-songwriter Joni Mitchell has officially become a U.S. citizen. The announcement has drawn mixed reactions given her outspoken political…

image.caption: Joni Mitchell, pictured at the 2026 Juno Awards in Hamilton, Ont., is now an American citizen, after living in the U.S. for 62 years. (Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

More than six decades after leaving Canada, legendary singer-songwriter Joni Mitchell has officially become a U.S. citizen. The announcement has drawn mixed reactions given her outspoken political views.
Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posted footage of citizenship ceremony to social media
More than six decades after leaving Canada, legendary singer-songwriter Joni Mitchell has officially become a U.S. citizen.
The 82-year-old artist shared the news on Instagram and X on Tuesday, posting a photo and video from her naturalization ceremony.

In the image, Mitchell is seen smiling and wearing a red beret and sunglasses, holding a small American flag with stars and stripes pinned to her cardigan. The second slide shows a video of her being applauded as she steps forward at the ceremony.
Her caption was brief: "A journey that began 62 years ago."
CBC News reached out to Mitchell's representatives, but did not hear back. CBC News found no further explanation of her decision elsewhere.
Born Roberta Joan Anderson in Fort Macleod, Alta., in 1943, Mitchell moved to the United States in the mid-1960s during a brief marriage to American musician Chuck Mitchell.
She lived in Detroit and New York before settling in California, where she became a defining figure in the Laurel Canyon music scene.
While she now resides in Santa Barbara, Calif., she continues to maintain a second residence on British Columbia’s Sunshine Coast.
Mitchell is known for songs like Big Yellow Taxi and Woodstock and for the 1971 album Blue, widely regarded as one of her landmark works.
Mitchell’s career has seen her evolve from a folk singer in Toronto coffee houses to one of the most influential songwriters in history.
With 19 studio albums, her accolades include 11 Grammys, five Juno Awards and induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

items: Joni Mitchell: 20 things you didn't know about one of Canada's greatest musicians
Junos 2026: Joni Mitchell, Rush make Junos history, the Beaches take home record-breaking win

blocks.text: Given Mitchell's vocal political stances in recent years, the timing of her U.S. citizenship has sparked some curiosity. According to a press release posted on her website, at a 2024 Hollywood Bowl performance, Mitchell used an expletive to describe U.S. President Donald Trump and urged the crowd to vote.

"I wish I could vote [in the U.S.]. I’m Canadian," she told the audience at the time. "I’m one of those lousy immigrants." She did not say whether that experience influenced her decision to become a U.S. citizen.
The transition to citizenship does not mean a parting of ways with her home country. Canada and the U.S. allow for dual citizenship, meaning Mitchell will retain her Canadian passport.
Mitchell’s decision to become a U.S. citizen has drawn mixed reactions on social media. Some celebrated the news. On X, user @NicoFranckerdk called it a "special moment for Joni."
X user @NicoFranckerdk celebrates Joni Mitchell’s announcement that she has become a U.S. citizen. (NicoFranckerdk/X)
X user @CanadaLinty wrote, "Just in time to vote in the midterms. Welcome aboard from another Cdn expat."
Others questioned the timing of the announcement amid strained U.S.-Canada relations and Mitchell's outspoken criticism of Trump.
X user @QueenofLaundry expressed her disapproval, writing "What?! Jesus READ THE ROOM Joni! Not impressed at all."
X user @QueenofLaundry expressed disapproval of Mitchell’s news. (@QueenofLaundry/X)
X user @FDelicioso wrote, "Never did I think I’d see Joni Mitchell be so completely tone deaf."
After a 2015 brain aneurysm impacted her speech and mobility, Mitchell spent years in recovery before returning to public performance in 2022.
In March, Prime Minister Mark Carney presented her with a lifetime achievement award at the Juno Awards in Hamilton, Ont.

As Mitchell officially joins the ranks of American citizens, the world may soon see her life story on the big screen. According to IMDb, a biopic is reportedly in development, with director Cameron Crowe and actor Meryl Streep attached to the project.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Christine Pagulayan is a Toronto-based producer and writer with CBC News, currently with the Entertainment unit. She has worked in various roles at CBC News Network and The National. She has also worked as a multiplatform reporter in Toronto, Winnipeg, Halifax and Moncton. You can reach her at christine.pagulayan@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Cornell president acknowledges he knew about fraternity sexual assault but didn’t follow up
articles.summary:
Michael Kotlikoff addressed his administration’s handling of the 2024 allegations as he faces calls for his resignation

Michael Kotlikoff, the president of Cornell University, has spoken to…

blocks.text: Michael Kotlikoff, the president of Cornell University, has spoken to the New York Times about sexual assault allegations at the school, acknowledging for the first time that he knew a student had reported being sexually assaulted in November 2024, but did not follow up with the Jane Doe involved in the months after learning about the alleged assault.
He also revealed that he did not know she had dropped out of Cornell until she filed a lawsuit last month.
Kotlikoff addressed his administration’s handling of the 2024 allegations as the university faces mounting scrutiny and calls for his resignation.

“The fact that Jane Doe experienced what she experienced at Cornell is something that I am personally sorry for,” Kotlikoff said in the interview, his first since the woman filed her civil lawsuit last month. “And I think this entire campus is sorry that occurred.
“I’ve heard enough from the community that there is a loss of trust,” he added. “People are angry. I understand that anger.”

Last month, a former student, identified in court documents by the pseudonym “Jane Doe”, filed a civil lawsuit against multiple parties, including the university, accusing seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity of sexually assaulting her at a party at their fraternity house on campus in October 2024. All of the men named in the lawsuit have denied wrongdoing, and none have been criminally charged.

The woman reported the incident to the Cornell University police department in November 2024. According to records obtained by the New York Times, after an internal investigation at Cornell, two of the men were expelled, two were suspended, and another, who had already graduated, was barred from campus. The remaining men received lighter punishments, which included an order to not contact Jane Doe, and to write “reflection papers”.
At the time, the Tompkins county district attorney declined to bring charges against the men, saying that there was not sufficient evidence.

The district attorney has since said that he would reopen his office’s investigation, and Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, said she was appointing Letitia James, the state’s attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the claims.
Kotlikoff called the allegations “deeply disturbing” in a statement earlier this month, and said he welcomed Hochul’s decision to appoint James to the case.
During the 90-minute interview, he was asked to respond to the criticisms that his administration had failed to respond to the former student’s allegations until she filed a lawsuit.
Kotlikoff pointed to a presidential taskforce that was established to examine sexual assault on campus.
He added, “I do think it’s important to understand we have more information now than we had at that time. We’ve learned some more information that has come out around how this process unfolded.”
Cornell’s faculty senate is expected to hold a rare vote of no confidence in the president later this month, according to reports.
In the interview, Kotlikoff also said that he had not been aware that the former student had left the school.

“I do think there’s an argument for what you said, which is that if in fact a student has withdrawn because she feels unsafe at the outcome of the” university’s administrative review process “or there’s specific concerns around individuals – you know that there were no-contact orders for those individuals – I think that’s something that leadership should be made aware of. I would agree with that.”

On Tuesday, after the interview, Kotlikoff announced that Cornell would suspend parties at fraternity houses for the remainder of the academic year. The university also said it planned to add experienced sexual assault investigators to work with its police force in response.

A newly formed special committee of the Cornell University Board of Trustees also announced that it had retained Sally Yates, who was a deputy attorney general in the Obama administration, to “lead a comprehensive independent review of how the university prevents and responds to sexual harassment, sexual assault and related misconduct on campus”.

items: Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

articles.title: Kenya confirms second Ebola case as relative of country's first victim
articles.summary: It follows the death last week of a man who had arrived in Kenya after travelling from DR Congo.

blocks.text: The 40-year-old Kenyan man who died on 5 October was diagnosed with Ebola shortly after being admitted to hospital in the capital, Nairobi.
A relative had taken him there shortly after picking him up at the airport. He had travelled from DR Congo, through Uganda to Kenya without his illness being detected.
Since his death, officials had determined that he had been in contact with 128 people - and since Tuesday 113 of them had been found, the health ministry said.
Of these, 108 were in quarantine in Kenya and tracing of the remaining 15 continued, it said.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

The current outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

articles.title: Sir Trevor Phillips encouraged CBS News colleagues to tell critics to ‘fuck off’
articles.summary:
Phillips sought to buck up his fellow London bureau colleagues during a contentious staff meeting on Tuesday

The veteran British broadcaster Sir Trevor Phillips had some strong words of…

blocks.text: The veteran British broadcaster Sir Trevor Phillips had some strong words of advice for his CBS News colleagues when facing off against critics who question the editorial integrity of the network: “Why don’t you just fuck off and let us do our jobs?”

Phillips made his blunt suggestion during a contentious meeting of the network’s London bureau on Tuesday, during which the foreign editor, Shayndi Raice, went on a lengthy tirade criticizing unnamed staffers for suggesting that editorial oversight amounted to “interference” and informing colleagues that disobeying editors would be insubordination and “legal grounds for firing”.

Phillips’s decision to join CBS was announced in June. It came after its billionaire owner, David Ellison, installed the opinion journalist and broadcast newcomer Bari Weiss as editor-in-chief in a move that shook staff.

The Guardian, which first reported the Tuesday meeting, reviewed an audio recording of the contentious session that rattled staffers. A CBS News spokesperson and Phillips declined to comment on the meeting.

Phillips spoke up initially to defend Raice, saying that the message she was delivering was common sense. “I’m genuinely surprised that you had to say anything that you just said in the last 15 minutes,” he said during the meeting. “It just seems to be axiomatic in any organization … I did want to say that I’m kind of surprised that in an organization of this vintage and capability, with the clever people I’ve met around here, that any of this actually has to be said.”

He then turned to outside opinion about CBS, telling colleagues that he faced criticism after it was announced he was leaving his perch at Sky News to serve as the network’s senior global affairs correspondent. Phillips is also a contributor to CBS’s flagship news show 60 Minutes, and voiced a short piece on Sunday on protests in Europe. Since CBS parent Paramount Global was acquired by Ellison’s Skydance Media in the summer of 2025, the company’s leadership has faced accusations of tilting the editorial scales in a more conservative-friendly direction.

“I could spend the next hour telling you the number of people when it was announced that I was coming here, the number of people who told me for all of the reasons you just explained, why this is the end of my career and how I was going to destroy everything that I’ve ever created, and all of that bollocks,” Phillips said.

He continued: “I think we’re in a new game now, actually, where we are now players as journalists. And what people are constantly trying to do is to knock us off – to frighten us, essentially, into doing this or doing that. It puts a premium on two things – one is our objectivity, and two: having each other’s backs. I think the worst thing that can happen now is if we start to go about telling people, ‘Well, I would have done this if the higher-ups hadn’t told me to do that.’ That’s exactly what everybody wants us to get into the game of. That’s how we become vulnerable. That’s how we start adjusting our copy according to somebody else’s lines outside of here … I think what you said is really, really important, but it points me in the direction of us having the mentality – forgive my French here – of telling everybody, ‘Why don’t you just fuck off and let us do our jobs?’”

articles.title: 3rd member of Canadian Armed Forces charged in kidnapping probe: Toronto police
articles.summary: A third member of the Canadian Armed Forces, and four other people, were arrested and charged in a kidnapping probe that led to the arrest of two other members of Canada’s military reserves, Toronto…

image.caption: Police recovered at least four firearms, 2,700 rounds of ammunition and large quantities of cocaine, methamphetamine and other controlled substances during the investigation. (Keira Mahoney/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto·New

A third member of the Canadian Armed Forces, and four other people, were arrested and charged in a kidnapping probe that led to the arrest of two other members of Canada’s military reserves, Toronto police announced Wednesday.
2 other military reserve members, 4 civilians also arrested and charged, police say

Joe Matthews, chief superintendent with Toronto Police Services, said the accused were arrested following an investigation that started while looking into a kidnapping on July 25. Police allege the victim was confined in the car at gunpoint, handcuffed and was assaulted as suspects tried to access cryptocurrency assets.

items: 2 Canadian Armed Forces members arrested in organized crime, kidnapping probe, DND says

blocks.text: Jack Miley, a 24-year-old from Toronto and reserve member of the CAF, was arrested on Sept. 24 and is facing seven charges including kidnapping for ransom with a firearm, forcible confinement and a number of firearm charges, said Matthews.

Earlier this month, police announced Talarambage Fernando and James Moreau, both reserve members of the 7 Toronto Regiment, were arrested on Aug. 11 in relation to the same investigation. Miley is a member of a different regiment, police said Wednesday.
Four civilians were also arrested, police said.

Police recovered at least four firearms during the investigation and 2,700 rounds of ammunition, about half of them blanks, were allegedly stolen from the military. They also found large quantities of cocaine, methamphetamine and other controlled substances.

Fernando, 22, and Moreau, 29, are facing a combined total of 49 charges, police said following their arrest. The pair have since been removed from their duties and their access to military facilities and bases has been restricted, according to the Department of National Defence.

Both have been charged with kidnapping for ransom, forcible confinement, unauthorized possession of a firearm in a motor vehicle, use of a firearm during the commission of an indictable offence, and mischief interfere with property.

Matthews said it’s not clear how the seven accused all knew each other, but said that’s part of the ongoing investigation. He said there’s nothing to indicate the accused are tied to any larger organized crime circles.

articles.title: UK’s ‘incoherent’ approach to China plagued by a lack of expertise, report says
articles.summary:
International grouping of China-sceptic legislators warns of risks inherent in misjudging bilateral relationship

The UK’s approach to China is “beset by incoherence” and plagued by a lack of…

blocks.text: The UK’s approach to China is “beset by incoherence” and plagued by a lack of senior expertise, according to a report warning of the risks inherent in misjudging the bilateral relationship.

Wednesday’s audit by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (Ipac), an international grouping of China-sceptic legislators, says past engagement with Beijing has often exposed the UK to the risks of interference without delivering the opportunities promised.

“Successful UK engagement with China must always be framed by an understanding that the PRC (People’s Republic of China) is an inherently hostile authoritarian state that does not share our values,” an underlined sentence in the audit reads.
The inherent power imbalance in the relationship with the world’s second largest economy is “further compounded by muddled policy and weak engagement”, it says.

It cites the example of a visiting Chinese delegation who had noted that no one who engaged with Beijing at a senior level in government was a Mandarin speaker, or had significant experience of living in China.
Although British expertise exists, it is often siloed and “not translated into capability”, Ipac, which counts members from all the UK’s major parties, says.

In an endorsement, the former security minister Tom Tugendhat said the report was “a clear-eyed and realistic take on the defining foreign policy problem of this century, filling a gap left by years of policy neglect”.
While the report accepts that “disengagement was not an option”, it advocates for clearly defined red lines around issues such as critical infrastructure, frontier technologies, and human rights.
The document offers several recommendations, including better institutional coordination, the strengthened use of national security tools, and diversification of supply chains.
It identifies emerging technologies such as AI as posing new challenges, in terms of disinformation and surveillance capabilities.
The climate crisis is identified as a low-risk area for cooperation and alignment.

“Climate targets as set will not be met without cooperation with China, and accepting medium term dependence. This means accepting supply chains tainted by forced labour and unfair trade practices,” the audit says.
The Guardian has contacted the UK government and the Chinese embassy in London for comment.

It was “very welcome” that there was an understanding that better language skills were needed to deal with China, said Kerry Brown, a former diplomat and director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London.
However, he said, “the critical issue now is lived experience” in China.
“Some of the members of Ipac … are really keen on promoting this very security-oriented idea that going to China is in some ways opening you up to exposure,” he said.

“You can’t teach really important things in a classroom;, you can only go and learn them through daily life … and that is the thing that is very difficult to do now, and it’s also the thing that doesn’t seem to be supported.”

articles.title: Trump administration promises social security recipients 3.6% increase in 2027
articles.summary:
‘Seniors have spent years watching their expenses outpacing their benefits’ advocate says

Social security recipients will…

blocks.text: Social security recipients will see a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (Cola) in 2027, increasing retirement benefits by an average of $75 per month as millions of Americans continue to grapple with rising prices.

Nearly 72 million social security beneficiaries will see higher payments beginning in January 2027, while approximately 7.3 million supplemental security income (SSI) recipients will receive increased payments starting on 31 December 2026, according to the Social Security Administration.
“Social security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability,” SSA commissioner Frank J Bisignano said on Wednesday.

Consumer prices climbed at an annual rate of 3.7% in September, up from 3.4% in August, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Inflation has reached its highest level since hitting a three-year peak of 4.2% in May. Gasoline prices rose 34% from last year, accounting for more than half of the overall price increases and driven largely by the US’s war on Iran. Fuel oil costs jumped 74% while air travel prices increased 22.4%.
Although social security increases are meant to keep up with inflation, they often do not cover rising costs like healthcare, housing and prescription drugs, particularly for senior citizens.
“Seniors have spent years watching their expenses outpacing their benefits,” Shannon Benton, director of the advocacy group Senior Citizens League, told NBC.
Pointing to the Cola adjustment, Benton said: “This provides a little breathing room but won’t undo the damage of what we’ve seen this decade.”
Aside from the pandemic, September’s inflation rate was the highest recorded ahead of a midterm election since 1990.

Wednesday’s announcement comes as a new Pew Research survey found that 44% of Americans struggled to afford at least one basic necessity over the past year, including medical care, transportation, housing or food. Some also reported getting food from a food bank or pantry.

With the midterm elections approaching, the survey also found that 61% of Americans believe there is too much economic inequality in the US. That view was more common among Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents (78%) than Republicans and Republican-leaning independents (42%).

articles.title: Turkey: Government raids, takes over top news channel
articles.summary: Turkish authorities have raided the Istanbul offices of Halk TV, halting broadcasts, appointing a trustee and opening an investigation. It is the latest chapter of a decadeslong media capture by…

image.caption: Authorities raided Halk TV and cut from live news to a Turkish film classic from 1973Image: ANKA

blocks.text: Turkish authorities took control of Halk TV on Wednesday — raiding the outlet's Istanbul studios, cutting all broadcasts and appointing a government trustee to oversee the company during an investigation into alleged corruption.

"Police raid at Halk TV headquarters! A trustee [manager] has been appointed, broadcasts have been halted," posted the popular news channel on X as police guarded the building, financial crimes agents searched offices and computers, and technicians cut live news channel feeds and YouTube broadcasts.
Footage posted online showed the moment the channel's live broadcast feed was cut — during an interview about a huge investment-fund scandal — and replaced with a classic Turkish film from 1973.

blocks.caption: Police surrounded Halk TV's Istanbul studio early Wednesday morningImage: ANKA

blocks.text: In a statement, the Istanbul Prosecutor's Office announced that Halk TV owner Cafer Mahiroglu is under investigation for "bribery, tender-rigging, ‌and laundering of assets derived ⁠from ⁠crime."
Government trustees were installed at Halk TV and other companies owned by Mahiroglu.
In all, prosecutors say 17 detention warrants were issued, with 11 individuals taken into custody.

Mahiroglu, who lives abroad and is being sought by authorities, decried what he called "a dark day for Turkey" and blasted the allegations against him as "baseless" in a video posted on X. The pro-opposition broadcaster said seven of his relatives had been detained by authorities.
"The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons," he said. "Using the judiciary as a weapon is the greatest harm inflicted on Turkey."
German gov't 'deeply concerned' about DW journalist's arrest
Erdogan smothering all press dissent in Turkey
Press freedom groups and opposition parties joined Mahiroglu in condemning the government takeover as the latest step by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to silence his critics.
Ozgur Ozel, leader of the main opposition New Party, said the raid was an abuse of government power.

Ozel called the raids "weak and cowardly," saying it was no coincidence they occurred just as jailed Erdogan opponent, Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, was set to make headlines delivering his defense in a sprawling graft trial.
"Raiding a television channel at dawn and appointing a trustee is an act only dictators would commit," Ozel wrote on X. "Unfortunately, this is the state to which they have reduced our country."
Press freedom has suffered dramatically during Erdogan's 22 years in power.
In the most recent Reporters Without Borders world press freedom index Turkey ranked 163 of 180 countries.
Istanbul's suspended mayor Imamoglu on trial
Similar pattern as Erdogan government eats up one media outlet after another

Ankara-based Contemporary Journalists Association decried the action against Halk TV, stating: "The appointment of a trustee at Halk TV and the suspension of its broadcast constitute a grave intervention against press freedom and freedom of expression. This decision, which disregards constitutional rights and the public's right to access information, is unacceptable."
Halk TV's takeover made it the fifth major Turkish news outlet forcefully put under trusteeship, ​following similar situations at Flash TV, Eko Turk, Haberturk and Tele1.
Veysel Ok, co-director of media-rights watchdog MLSA, said the intervention against Halk TV was "one of the most significant steps in the government's efforts to monopolize the flow of information."

"Halk TV's position as the most-watched news channel also reveals the real target of this intervention: Depriving the public of its right to access news from different sources," Ok told French news agency AFP.
"Defending press freedom means defending the public's right to learn the truth, hold the government to account and freely decide its own future."

The European Parliament's Turkey rapporteur Nacho Sanchez Amor criticized the move on X, saying the government was clearly "not happy with controlling 90% of media" and was instead "aiming for the 100%."
"Amidst detentions of journalists & broad online censorship, freedom of media & expression will soon be just a memory."

articles.title: Hunger rises to 22.6% in Q3 – SWS
articles.summary: More Filipinos experienced involuntary hunger in the third quarter of the year, according to a Social Weather Stations survey.

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 12:00am
Results of the Sept. 21 to 27 survey released Wednesday showed that 22.6 percent of respondents experienced being hungry and having nothing to eat at least once in the past three months.
KJ Rosales
MANILA, Philippines — More Filipinos experienced involuntary hunger in the third quarter of the year, according to a Social Weather Stations survey.
It went up slightly from 20.3 percent in June, but still below the 23.2 percent in March.
The latest hunger rate comprises 16.2 percent of respondents who said their families experienced moderate hunger (from 15.8 percent) and 6.4 percent who experienced severe hunger (from 4.5 percent).
Moderate hunger is experienced “only once” or “a few times” in the last three months, while severe hunger is “often” or “always” in the last three months.

Across areas, the September hunger rate was highest among respondents in Metro Manila at 27 percent (from 21 percent), followed by those in Mindanao at 23.7 percent (from 24 percent), rest of Luzon at 23.6 percent (from 17.3 percent) and the Visayas at 16 percent (from 22.3 percent).

Involuntary hunger increased among poor households, from 24.5 percent to 27.9 percent and from 29.9 percent, while it was steady among not poor or borderline poor respondents, from 16.1 percent to 16.2 percent.

The photo of the Commission on Audit's office in Quezon City.
The STAR / Michael Varcas

MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan was called out for failing to justify with proper documentation its expenses related to overseas trips of its justices and personnel, as well as organizing events in four-star and five-star venues across the country.

In its annual audit report for the anti-graft court in 2025 published on its website yesterday, the Commission on Audit (COA) reported the “granting and liquidation of CAs (cash advances) for official foreign travels of SB officials and employees for CY (calendar year) 2025, totaling P11,869,847.98, were not fully supported with complete documentary requirements.”

The amount was disbursed for seven foreign trips – mostly conferences and training – to the US state of Missouri; Victoria, Australia; Budapest, Hungary; Dubai, United Arab Emirates; Doha in Qatar and Singapore from September to December 2025, according to the COA report.
It noted that the costliest trips were the ones in Hungary at over P2.5 million, Dubai at over P1.88 million and Singapore at over P1.82 million.

“Review of the above-listed CAs revealed that the documentary requirements for granting the said CAs such as: (a) letters of invitation; (b) plane fare quotations and (c) flight itineraries were not submitted,” the COA noted.
From the total amount of over P11.8 million, over P7.1 million lacked narrative reports.

Meanwhile, the cost of roundtrip tickets to Hungary worth P621,783 for the attendance of “three justices” to “a special course” on artificial intelligence in criminal legal profession “could not be determined if within the allowable rates prescribed for foreign travels of officials” under relevant policies of the Sandiganbayan.

According to the anti-graft court’s rules cited by COA, only the presiding justice is entitled to “full business class” while the rest of its workforce should take only “official economy class” in case flights would not be subsidized by the host country or sponsoring organization.

The state auditor also flagged the Sandiganbayan’s “lease of privately-owned venues for various official activities,” which was “not consistently supported with the required justifications and documentary evidence.”

The anti-graft court “entered into 12 contracts with private lessors under negotiated procurement,” wherein a total of P13,649,836.40 was spent to use “mostly five-star and four-star hotels… within and outside Metro Manila” for its various events that included seminars, workshops and its Christmas party in 2025.

Most of the funds were disbursed for the anti-graft court’s “executive briefing and capacity building” held at the heritage-themed Las Casas Filipinas de Acuzar resort in Bagac, Bataan with a bill of P5,175,200.

Other activities – including a tree-planting that was included in a special en banc session – were held at five-star hotels, namely Clark Marriott Hotel in Pampanga and Baguio Country Club, and at four-star Seda Vertis North hotel in Quezon City.

“Further examination of DVs (disbursement vouchers) and supporting records disclosed that several transactions were processed without submission of required documents necessary to demonstrate prior consideration of available government-owned venues, written justification establishing that the lease of privately-owned venues was more economical and efficient, or justification supporting the use of four- or five-star hotels,” the COA said.

articles.title: NBI tags 10 persons of interest in Laos drug haul
articles.summary: The National Bureau of Investigation has identified 10 persons and entities of interest in the seizure of 512 kilograms of suspected shabu in Laos, which authorities believe was intended for shipment…

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 12:00am
The NBI vowed to pursue everyone responsible for or involved in the alleged attempt to smuggle the drugs worth P3.5 billion into the country.
PNA / File photo

MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has identified 10 persons and entities of interest in the seizure of 512 kilograms of suspected shabu in Laos, which authorities believe was intended for shipment to the Philippines.
The shipment, which was reportedly bound for the Philippines on a private jet, was intercepted on Oct. 1 by Laotian authorities.
The Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) has identified two Filipinos allegedly involved in the plan to transport the drugs.
One of them, identified as Dibaroson Fahad from Marawi, has been arrested and is being investigated for alleged links to a Davao-based drug syndicate.

The other suspect, identified only as Boyet, allegedly chartered the aircraft and paid for it through a bank transfer. However, the PDEA said he left the country for Hong Kong a day before the operation.
At a press briefing on Monday, PDEA chief Isagani Nerez said traffickers may have shifted to air transport after repeated maritime interdictions disrupted their operations.
The drugs were believed to be intended for Metro Manila.
BOC gathers information
Meanwhile, Bureau of Customs Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno said the BOC has gathered information about the shabu shipment.

At yesterday’s Kapihan sa Manila Bay news forum, Nepomuceno said he received information on reported attempts to bring illegal drugs into the country, but would leave it to the PDEA to disclose the information.
“To be honest, I have some information already and details but I would respect PDEA in handling it. By law, PDEA is the primary agency. I do not want to preempt,” said Nepomuceno.
He said someone shared information on “who they talked to, who hired the airplanes and how many times this happened. We already have the information,” he added.

Nepomuceno said based on the information gathered by intelligence officers, it has happened before and the drug suspects allegedly used private planes to transport the contraband and that their planes landed in “private hangars of private companies.”
“We would be looking into that,” he added.
The BOC will review the current setup with hangars for private planes, some catering to “VVIP” (very, very important persons) that may include businessmen and politicians.
He said while the BOC has personnel assigned to these private hangars, they might have been intimidated by the presence of VVIPs.

“So, I will see how we could strengthen the BOC’s capability with these private companies. I just hope that our VVIPs, from the business sector and political sector, would not get mad. I hope that when we fix the entry and exits for private hangars, they would not take it out on our people,” Nepomuceno said.

He added, “Let us admit that these areas are sensitive because this is where the super VVIPs pass through. We cannot just impose our own rules. We would respect the sensibilities and sensitivities of these private entrances and exits. But we would have to do our job.” – Evelyn Macarian

articles.title: VP Sara told: Stop playing victim
articles.summary: As her legal team prepares to take its turn in presenting her side in the impeachment trial, Vice President Sara Duterte should focus on building up her defense instead of portraying herself as a…

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — As her legal team prepares to take its turn in presenting her side in the impeachment trial, Vice President Sara Duterte should focus on building up her defense instead of portraying herself as a victim, private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan said yesterday.
“They always play the victim card. So again, let us remove that ‘kawawa naman ang VP syndrome’,” Kapunan said.
“She is not the victim, the public is the victim here. You’re talking about public funds. You’re talking about a public officer and impeachment,” she said.

“She should start presenting or building up her case. She should start talking to her father so that she is able to explain the accounts of the father and herself. She should start talking to her husband,” she said, referring to detained former president Rodrigo Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio.

The veteran lawyer argued that attention should focus on the hundreds of millions in the bank accounts and assets of Duterte and her family. “Whose money is this? These are public funds,” she pointed out.
Malacañang said it’s not questioning the move of the prosecution.

“Well, everybody, we are all for the truth. We are all for transparency and accountability. But if it’s the legal strategy of the prosecution, we cannot question whatever decision they make,” Palace press officer Claire Castro said.
Castro believes the evidence and documents presented relating to the withdrawn articles would likely to stay in the minds of Filipinos, although the Vice President can address them in various ways.
Citing records, prosecution witness accountant-lawyer Alexander Cabrera earlier confirmed the existence of P817.87 million in unexplained wealth of Duterte and her spouse.
He emphasized his figure was conservative, as the amount could reach P1.5 billion between 2022 and 2025 if other documents were included in his analysis.

House of Representatives impeachment team adviser and spokesman Robert Ace Barbers, meanwhile, maintained that the prosecution’s withdrawal of three of four cases against Duterte did not deprive her of due process.

“They (defense counsels) were given the opportunity to cross-examine our witnesses. The defense was also given the chance to examine or scrutinize the documentary evidence that we all presented,” Barbers pointed out.

The prosecution has opted to proceed solely with Article II, which covers allegations of unexplained wealth, discrepancies in Duterte’s asset declarations and the alleged retention of business interests in violation of constitutional restrictions.

“They were allowed to make the necessary reply. And that is the real essence of due process. That’s why I don’t know where Senator-Judge Cayetano is coming from when he said that due process will be sacrificed here,” he said.
For retired Supreme Court associate justice Noel Tijam, the dropping of the three Articles of Impeachment would “fortify suspicion that the impeachment court is a kangaroo court.”

“With the dropping of the three Articles of Impeachment against the Vice President, the spotlight has been refocused no longer solely on the Vice President but on Congress, the ombudsman and the executive department,” Tijam wrote on Facebook.
He added that the development would also spawn perception that the impeachment court “is weak and condescending to the defense and subservient to the prosecution.”

Meanwhile, Sen. Panfilo Lacson debunked Duterte spokesman Paolo Panelo’s claim that up to P500 million in public funds had been wasted hearing two Articles of Impeachment that were later withdrawn by the prosecution.

Lacson said the Senate’s budget for the ongoing impeachment trial was sourced from the P27.5-million continuing appropriations in last year’s national budget, when the first impeachment complaint was filed and later voided by the Supreme Court.

“Where did he get his P25M/day figure? As far as I know, the GAA 2025 budget for the impeachment trial, most of which has remained unspent (only roughly P2 million was disbursed for the judges’ robes and other items) from the original P27.5 million, is now being used under the ‘continuing appropriations’ provision in the General Appropriations Act,” Lacson said.
Lacson said Panelo might be referring to the Senate’s P25-million daily operating cost. - Ghio Ong, Marc Jayson Cayabyab, Helen Flores

articles.title: Government rolls out water filters amid ‘super’ El Niño
articles.summary: The government will start distributing free portable water filtration kits to communities next week to ensure adequate supply of potable water amid a looming super El Niño, Social Welfare…

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The government will start distributing free portable water filtration kits to communities next week to ensure adequate supply of potable water amid a looming super El Niño, Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian announced yesterday.
At a Palace briefing, Gatchalian and officials of the Department of Social Welfare and Development demonstrated the use of the filtration kits, which are intended for household and community use.
Gatchalian said the government has a stockpile of the Sawyer water filtration system with bucket adapter kits supplied by international nongovernment organization Waves for Water.
The system is certified by the Department of Health as a medical device and has passed the Philippine National Standards for Drinking Water.
It uses 0.1-micron filters that can remove bacteria associated with cholera, salmonella, E. coli and coliform contamination from deep wells, springs and rainwater.
The DSWD will launch the filtration system in Tondo, Manila next week, prioritizing areas under a state of calamity and densely populated communities in Metro Manila.

Larger filtration systems equipped with rain catchers and faucets are also being deployed and operated as community drinking water stations in San Felipe, Zambales and Mayantoc, Tarlac, while similar facilities have been used in Batanes.
Other government agencies are also stepping up efforts to mitigate the effects of El Niño.

The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), for its part, is promoting nature-based solutions to help farms withstand drought, including bamboo plantations to retain soil moisture, soil conservation structures to prevent erosion and small water impounding systems to provide alternative water supplies.
The department is also working with irrigation agencies and local communities to improve water management and promote sustainable farming practices.

The Philippine National Police (PNP), meanwhile, has ordered police camps, stations and regional headquarters to adopt “water-smart” protocols, conserve water, install rainwater harvesting systems and repair leaking infrastructure.
A fast lane for legally imported agricultural products is also being considered by the Bureau of Customs (BOC) to speed up the release of food supplies and help prevent shortages amid El Niño.

“We have to double the facilitation of imported food items especially during El Niño, if there would be a shortage in rice and vegetables,” BOC Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno said at a forum yesterday.
He added that the agency would explore the proposal and support the Department of Agriculture (DA)’s programs, provided importers have complete permits and comply with requirements.
P6.5 billion losses
Barely a month since the super El Niño started, agricultural losses from the El Niño have reached more than P6.539 billion, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council.
Citing DA data, the NDRRMC said the losses cover about 159,211 metric tons of totally and partially damaged crops.

Cagayan Valley recorded the biggest share with more than P4.967 billion in agricultural losses, followed by the Cordillera Administrative Region with P934.9 million and the Davao Region with P410 million.
The Zamboanga Peninsula reported P95.8 million in losses, followed by Bicol with P37.4 million and Central Visayas with P22.7 million.

Other affected regions include Caraga with P22 million, Calabarzon with P19.7 million, Soccsksargen with P12.5 million, Central Luzon with more than P1.8 million and Western Visayas with over P1.8 million.
As of Tuesday, the NDRRMC reported that 215,386 farmers and fisherfolk had been affected by the dry conditions in their farms and fishing grounds.
About 451,889 people have also been affected across various provinces, while 109 cities and municipalities have been placed under a state of calamity.
In response, the government has provided more than P46.4 million in food and non-food assistance to 36,275 affected families.
Inflation
The worsening dry conditions could drive up consumer prices and weigh on economic growth, Chinabank Research warned.
In a report, the bank estimated that inflation could exceed eight percent under a severe El Niño scenario.
“We expect inflation to peak in the fourth quarter of 2026 and remain below eight percent in our baseline, although a severe El Niño could push it above that level,” Chinabank said.
The bank said reduced production of rice, corn and other crops would likely be the most immediate source of price pressures.
Higher electricity demand and constraints on water and hydropower supplies could also contribute to inflation.

“With inflation already elevated, a more severe El Niño remains a key upside risk to our inflation outlook,” the bank noted, adding that while earlier interest rate increases could help contain second-round price pressures, monetary tightening has limited ability to address inflation driven by supply disruptions. - Keisha Ta-asan, Michael Punongbayan, Josiah Antonio, Mark Ernest Villeza, Rainier Allan Ronda, Evelyn Macairan

articles.title: ‘House realigned P206 billion in 2027 national budget’
articles.summary: Senate finance committee chairman JV Ejercito has raised concerns over the House of Representatives’ realignments in the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027.

blocks.text: Headlines
October 15, 2026 | 12:00am

Ejercito expressed concern over the P130-billion reduction for foreign-assisted projects (FAP), which are funded through loan agreements with partners such as the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) and the Asian Development Bank (ADB).
Philstar.com / File
MANILA, Philippines — Senate finance committee chairman JV Ejercito has raised concerns over the House of Representatives’ realignments in the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027.
Ejercito noted that an estimated P206 billion was altered from the executive branch’s original spending plan and slashed funds for big-ticket infrastructure and preventive health care.
The allocation for FAPs is supposed to pay off the multibillion-peso loans from JICA and ADB that were used for big-ticket infrastructure projects including the Metro Manila Subway.
“There was noticeable slashing of funds for major programs, especially foreign-assisted programs,” Ejercito said.
“The more we delay, the bigger the problem gets. We have to finish all of these major infra so they can be put to use,” he added.
The Japanese government has sought clarifications from the Philippine government regarding delays in JICA-funded projects.

Ejercito also noted a P9.5-billion cut from the Calamity Fund amid looming threats from a strong El Niño, as well as an apparent shift toward short-term social assistance at the expense of preventive health care programs.

Under the Department of Health’s budget, the Health Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP) meant to improve hospitals was slashed by P4.5 billion, the immunization program lost P4 billion and health promotion programs were cut by P2 billion.
In contrast, allocations for the Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients (MAIFIP) surged by P23.9 billion.
MAIFIP is a controversial health care program, which has been criticized as a “discretionary fund” vulnerable to political patronage.

“It’s a puzzle to me because one of the key factors of the UHC (Universal Health Care) is to strengthen the preventive side. And they slashed it. What are we doing? We remove immunization and health promotion then when people get sick we provide medical assistance?” said Ejercito, a principal author of the UHC Act.
Flood control
In the Department of Public Works and Highways, right-of-way acquisitions were reduced by P2.6 billion while flood mitigation structures within major river basins saw a P4.6-billion cut.
Meanwhile, general construction and maintenance received an additional P13 billion and overall flood mitigation items were increased by P8.04 billion.
Ejercito cautioned against over-relying on unconditional subsidies, stressing that long-term infrastructure investment generates sustained employment.
“Budget process is a balancing act,” he said.

Ejercito announced that the finance committee received the official copy of the House General Appropriations Bill on Tuesday and copies were distributed to senators and committee vice chairs to begin scrutiny.

With only limited fiscal space left for Senate institutional amendments, Ejercito said the Senate would demand Regional Development Council approvals and disallow lump-sum allocations for flood control, prioritizing only uncompleted projects along major river basins and the top 10 flood-prone areas.
The finance committee set an Oct. 23 deadline for subcommittees to submit their reports, with civil society organizations and watchdogs scheduled for consultations on Oct. 26.
Ejercito plans to sponsor the committee report on Nov. 11, open plenary debates on Nov. 23 and targets the signing of the 2027 national budget by the second week of December.

articles.title: Duterte defense wants fewer witnesses, evidence
articles.summary: The defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte is not satisfied with the prosecution’s efforts to shorten its list of evidence and witnesses in his upcoming trial for crimes against…

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 12:00am
Former president Rodrigo Duterte attends the fourth status conference at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands, on Oct. 13, 2026.
International Criminal Court / Philstar.com's screenshot

MANILA, Philippines — The defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte is not satisfied with the prosecution’s efforts to shorten its list of evidence and witnesses in his upcoming trial for crimes against humanitbefore the International Criminal Court (ICC).
During the fourth status conference on Tuesday, defense lawyer Peter Haynes pointed out that some of the prosecution witnesses may be “filtered out” from the list.

“They include people who haven’t made a witness statement, people who give precisely similar evidence to other witnesses. They include witnesses with whom the prosecution hasn’t had any contact for a long period of time and witnesses who explicitly said they want nothing further to do with the proceedings,” he said.
But the prosecution maintained that they have already made efforts to shorten the time needed for them to present their evidence.

Trial lawyer Edward Jeremy said the prosecution has reclassified some of its intended witnesses, including filing a request for admission of prior recorded testimony instead of calling them to testify in person.
“With our latest reclassifications, we’ve saved 20 hours of court time. The 193 (hours) figure is now down to 173. We will continue to look at that list,” he told the judges.

Senior trial lawyer Julian Nicholls said they also do not expect to call all of those on the list, citing previous case where he said they “ended up dropping a lot of witnesses for different reasons.”

The final number of prosecution witnesses has yet to be released. But during the case’s first status conference in May, Nicholls said as many 70 witnesses may be presented against the former president during his trial.
These include 31 insider witnesses, 17 crime-base witnesses and 12 witnesses “who are relevant to explain the background and the contextual elements of the crimes charged.”
The prosecutor also intends to call 25 to 30 of these witnesses to give viva voce or verbal testimony during the trial.
Aside from the issue of witnesses, the parties also discussed the defense’s complaints over what it described as a “sheer volume of material” disclosed by the prosecution.
Duterte’s camp is asking the judges to order the prosecution to open a new case file to limit the number of disclosed items to just 10,000.

The trial chamber has yet to issue a written decision on the request, although presiding judge Joanna Korner noted during the hearing that imposing a cap could result in the prosecution violating its disclosure obligations. Duterte’s trial is expected to begin on Nov. 30.

articles.title: Pinoys trust journalists over vloggers – survey
articles.summary: Despite an expanded information environment, a survey on Tuesday found that journalists remain Filipinos’ main source of news.

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 12:00am
In a non-commissioned survey by Momentum Research, the public opinion research firm found that 83 percent of Filipino adults get their news from journalists working for news organizations.
STAR / Edd Gumban
MANILA, Philippines — Despite an expanded information environment, a survey on Tuesday found that journalists remain Filipinos’ main source of news.
In comparison, 32.3 percent had vloggers, influencers and content creators as news sources.
About three in four Filipino adults say they trust the news and information they get from journalists, while 18.4 percent say they do not.
This finding is consistent across regions, political affiliations and generations, Momentum Research said.
With the proliferation of disinformation and misleading generative artificial intelligence, the survey stressed that deciding which sources to trust “matters more than ever.”
Across age groups, 84.3 percent of Gen Z Filipinos trust journalists the most, followed by millennials at 78.9 percent, Gen X at 74 percent and baby boomers and the silent generation at 55.8 percent.
Distrust in content creators, influencers and vloggers accounted for between 62 and 67 percent.
In terms of political affiliations, trust is highest “among those who identify as pro-opposition” at 86.4 percent.
About seven in 10 indicated distrust in vloggers and creators.
Pro-Duterte adults have an approximately 20 percent distrust rate in journalists as a news source.
More than a third of Marcos and Duterte supporters trust news and information from content creators and vloggers, researchers found.
Journalists are most trusted in Luzon at 82.2 percent.
The Visayas posted a 74.5-percent trust in journalists.
Mindanao had 68.4 percent.
Despite Metro Manila posting a 73.6 percent trust in journalists, the capital accounted for the highest trust rating for content creators and vloggers at 39.2 percent.
Momentum Research said 1,487 Filipino adults participated in the study through face-to-face interviews.

articles.title: Legarda extends leave anew
articles.summary: Sen. Loren Legarda has asked for another extension of her medical leave abroad, Senate Secretary Renato Bantug Jr. confirmed yesterday.

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Loren Legarda has asked for another extension of her medical leave abroad, Senate Secretary Renato Bantug Jr. confirmed yesterday.
This marks Legarda’s second month of absence in the Senate as the ombudsman probes her and her son’s allegedly anomalous solar projects.
Legarda has been on leave since Aug. 3, missing out on her duties in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has accused Legarda of using her post to secure exclusive solar power franchises for her son Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste, resulting in multibillion-peso “ghost electricity” losses.
Authorities are probing Legarda, Leviste and former energy secretary Alfonso Cusi for plunder and graft.

Legarda’s spokesman Tony La Viña has denied the senator was running away from the charges, saying Legarda will go home soon and is willing to rejoin the Senate majority and abandon Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano’s bloc.
Sen. Panfilo Lacson said Legarda is welcome to join them, harboring no hard feelings for her for siding with Cayetano.

articles.title: VP to House prosecutors: Where’s the evidence?
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte believes that the House prosecutors had to withdraw three of the four cases in the ongoing Senate impeachment trial against her after failing to present strong evidence.

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 12:00am
Rep. Keith Flores (Bukidnon), a member of the prosecution, addresses the Senate impeachment court during Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial on Oct. 1, 2026.
Senate SMU

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte believes that the House prosecutors had to withdraw three of the four cases in the ongoing Senate impeachment trial against her after failing to present strong evidence.
“After all that, where is the evidence?” Duterte asked in her statement.

Presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero said the impeachment court has accepted the prosecution’s move to pursue only Article II on Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth and drop Article I on the unaccounted P612.5 million in confidential funds, Article III on bribery and Article IV on her grave threats against President Marcos, First Lady Liza Marcos and former House speaker Martin Romualdez.

“You threatened, intimidated and hauled OVP (Office of the Vice President) personnel to detention. You started impeachment with allegations but failed to establish them with compelling evidence,” said Duterte.

“You wielded the subpoena powers of the House of Representatives, yet failed to produce what was needed to substantiate your accusations. You then brought the Articles of Impeachment to the Senate, seemingly hoping that the impeachment trial would somehow make up for what was missing from the beginning,” she added.
Duterte said allegations of cash distribution and political maneuvering surrounding the 2027 national budget raise troubling questions.

“Is the budget being used to serve the Filipino people or has it become a bargaining chip to pressure senators who will sit as judges and reward those who vote ‘yes’ in the House of Representatives?” Duterte noted.
“The public deserves better than political theater disguised as accountability,” Duterte added.

Duterte said accountability should also be applied to President Marcos. “And if accountability is truly your battle cry, apply it consistently – even to the President, who is firm that a drug habit is not about accountability. Evidence, not arrogance. Genuine accountability, not political persecution,” Duterte added.
Prosecutors dropping three of the four cases against the Vice President is an admission that the allegations lacked basis from the start, according to Duterte’s spokesman Paolo Panelo.
Prosecutors defended the move, saying it aims to expedite the proceedings.
Conflict of interest

A counsel for Duterte said National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag looking into the allegations made by dismissed police officer Rodulfo Gracioso against Duterte is “heavily burdened with conflict of interest.”

Counsel Paul Lawrence Lim made the reaction after Matibag said the NBI is zeroing in on several properties linked to the Dutertes after finding major discrepancies in declared values in her statement of assets, liabilities and net worth and the agency’s initial estimates.
