articles.title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
articles.summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan had worked for the AI giant for more than a year before he was arrested by the FBI.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters/DOJ
A recording device (R) was wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into a TV (L)
ByLaura Cress
Technology reporter
A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".
As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.
But, here's we do know so far.
Help from a chatbot
The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).
Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.
Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".
The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.
Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.

The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.
Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.
But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.
Hiding in plain toilet paper
On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.
A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.
The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.
When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.
In a post on X, external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".
It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Alfozan was captured looking behind a television where a device had been inserted

blocks.text: Alfozan was captured looking behind a television where a device had been inserted
Who is Abdulrahman Alfozan?
Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.
Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream.

"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."

Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt."

On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.
The FBI investigation is ongoing.
If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£190,000) fine.

articles.title: Sally Rooney says she can no longer sell books in UK due to Palestine Action support
articles.summary:
Irish writer of Normal People says she can no longer receive royalties from British sales and she cancelled UK trip due to fear of arrest

Sally Rooney has said she is being forced to…

blocks.text: Sally Rooney has said she is being forced to withdraw her books from sale in the UK because of her support for the banned organisation Palestine Action.
The Irish novelist, whose books include Normal People and Conversations With Friends, said her public support for the direct action group meant she could no longer receive royalties from UK sales.

After Palestine Action was banned last year, Rooney said she would use proceeds from her sales to support Palestine Action. Supporting organisations banned under the Terrorism Act is an offence and she subsequently cancelled a trip to the UK to pick up an award, for fear of arrest.

In a statement provided to the Guardian, the bestselling author said: “‘In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK. The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland.

“As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence. After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK. I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences.”

In a high court statement in support of the legal challenge to proscription, warning against its impact on freedom of expression, Rooney said her books could disappear from UK stores and the publication of new works in the UK could be prevented.

Her books have been critically acclaimed – she has been described as the voice of a generation – and hugely commercially successful in the UK. Normal People has sold more than 1m copies, while Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World, Where Are You have each sold more than 500,000. Normal People and Conversations With Friends were adapted by the BBC, and the former racked up 62.7m views, becoming the broadcaster’s most-streamed series of 2020.

Rooney said last year that she had been advised by the independent producer of the TV dramatisations that any payment to her for those series, both broadcast before the ban, would be a breach of terrorism laws if it knew or suspected that she was using the royalties to fund Palestine Action.

Section 15 of the Terrorism Act makes it an offence if a person “provides money or other property, and knows or has reasonable cause to suspect that it will or may be used for the purposes of terrorism”. It carries a maximum sentence of 14 years in prison.

Her UK and Ireland publisher, Faber, said: “Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.

“As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format. We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories.”

More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK for alleged support of Palestine Action since it was banned in July last year, most for holding placards saying: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”

About 2,500 people have been charged, although none have been tried as a legal challenge to the ban is continuing and will be heard by the supreme court next month. Most arrests and charges have related to section 13 of the Terrorism Act, which carries a maximum jail term of six months.

Huda Ammori, a co-founder of Palestine Action who has brought the legal challenge against the ban, said: “Sally Rooney being unable to publish her work in the UK marks a new low in the escalating assault on free speech caused by the proscription of Palestine Action …

”[She] took a brave and principled stand from the moment plans to ban Palestine Action were announced. She has refused to compromise her convictions, even at considerable personal and professional cost. Her work should be celebrated and widely available​, not driven off the shelves of British bookshops because she refuses to be complicit in the suppression of solidarity with the Palestinian people. No author should have to choose between their principles and their freedom to publish.​”

Kerry Moscogiuri, the chief executive of Amnesty International UK, said: “Whatever one’s views on Palestine Action, we should all be concerned when laws intended to combat terrorism end up silencing artistic freedom and the ability to engage in peaceful political dissent.
“Writers should not find their books disappearing from shelves because of their political beliefs. Nor should people have to choose between expressing their conscience and pursuing their livelihoods.

“Sally Rooney’s willingness to accept the personal consequences of her convictions deserves recognition. There is a real danger that others, seeing the price she has paid, will decide they cannot afford to speak out.”
Rooney’s books were still on sale in central London on Wednesday afternoon, and Waterstones said that existing stock could still be sold.

Gian Carlo, a bookseller at Henry Pordes Books, said the same, adding: “Nothing goes to Sally Rooney in this case. We sell books of all types, they’re not connected to the author. I can’t say I don’t agree with her.

John Clegg, a bookseller at London Review Bookshop, said: “I ordered more as soon as I saw the news. I saw the number go down to zero, so I hope they go through. People are going to want them and we’re not going to be able to get them through Faber.
“Good on her for taking a stand, it seems a ridiculous law. If this thing convinces the Home Office to move faster to get rid of it, I’m all for it.”

articles.title: Pope Leo’s recovery from lung cancer surgery ‘progressing as planned’
articles.summary:
Pontiff has begun walking in his hospital room and is eating normally after operation to remove growth, doctors say

Pope Leo’s recovery from a lung cancer operation is progressing as…

blocks.text: Pope Leo’s recovery from a lung cancer operation is progressing as planned, his doctors have said, as the pontiff received good wishes from around the world, including a letter from Britain’s King Charles.

Leo, who had a cancerous mass removed from his right lung late on Tuesday, began walking in his hospital room after respiratory therapy on Wednesday. He was eating normally, his doctors Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritoria said in a statement issued by the Vatican.
A blood test and chest x-ray showed “normal post-operative progress” and the values were “within the expected range for the type of procedure performed”, they said.

The operation at Rome’s Gemelli hospital confirmed that Leo, 71, has the most common kind of lung cancer – adenocarcinoma. The Vatican has not yet disclosed the results of further tests to determine whether the cancer has spread and if more treatment will be needed.
The cancer diagnosis for Leo, who was elected the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church in May 2025, has come as a shock.

In a rare moment of Vatican transparency, the pope announced during his angelus prayer on Sunday that doctors had found a small nodule on his lung during a checkup, and that it was “well-contained” and detected early.

Messages have been sent from around the world. King Charles, who is also being treated for an undisclosed form of cancer, would write to Leo privately, a source told Agence France-Presse. Charles and Queen Camilla met the pope when they travelled to the Vatican in October last year.
Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, wished Leo a full and swift recovery in a message posted on X, and said the pontiff was “a source of hope and inspiration for billions around the world”.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said he and his wife, Jeanette, were praying for Leo. The couple met the pontiff at the Vatican in May. There has been no reaction yet from Donald Trump, who clashed with Leo earlier this year over the US-Israeli war in Iran, or from the US vice-president, JD Vance, a Catholic.
The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, wrote on X that Leo’s serenity and strength were an inspiration for all. “We hope for his full and speedy recovery,” she wrote

Before the operation, all of Leo’s appointments until 20 October had been cancelled. He went on a papal trip to France in September and is scheduled to go to South America in November for a 12-day trip covering 10 cities.

articles.title: Container ship sinks near strait of Hormuz amid surge in Iranian attacks
articles.summary:
Second vessel also reportedly sinking as uptick in strikes suggests Iran trying to close waterway before US elections

A container ship has ⁠sunk near the strait of Hormuz and a second cargo…

blocks.text: A container ship has ⁠sunk near the strait of Hormuz and a second cargo vessel was reportedly sinking amid the sharpest uptick in Iranian attacks on shipping since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran.

The surge of attacks suggests Iran is trying to fully close the strategic waterway in a deliberate attempt to frustrate Donald Trump’s efforts to bring down fuel prices before the US midterm elections on 3 November.
The Trump administration has been attempting to deflect attention from the economic impact of the war on Iran by blaming Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries for increased fuel prices.

On Wednesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported at least five incidents including drone strikes in the previous 48 hours targeting tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area.
“There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate,” one maritime security source said.

The Singapore-flagged GFS Pride ​container ‌ship sank on Wednesday after an attack the previous day while in a separate incident, the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao was also reported to be sinking close to the strait ⁠after being previously hit by a ​projectile ​on 23 September, maritime security sources said.
Apparently referring to the GFS Pride, Iran said a cargo ship sank after hitting a naval mine while travelling an unauthorised passage through the strait.
State television quoted a statement from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp (IRGC) that said the ship was traveling on what it called an “illegal and dangerous route” when it hit the mine.
The unidentified ship, which was shown tilted in the water and spewing a thick plume of smoke, was carrying 2,500 containers, the broadcast said.
However, the UKTMO suggested that both ships had been hit by unidentified projectiles, raising questions over Tehran’s account.

blocks.caption: People walk past an anti-US billboard in Tehran depicting an IRGC member placing his foot on a US unmanned underwater vehicle. Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPA

blocks.text: Iran has repeatedly warned ships from trying to transit through the strait without its approval. The US military has been guiding ships through the waterway on a route nearer to Oman’s coast.
The latest attacks come as ships in the area were reporting an intense series of attacks in recent days with six vessels attacked on Sunday alone, according to UKTMO’s monitoring.
Analysis by the Financial Times said 24 ships were hit in the two weeks to 11 October. Of the vessels hit, three were refined energy product tankers while two others were crude oil tankers.

The increased tempo of Iranian attacks appears to have caused a dramatic drop off in oil shipments through the strait, as Tehran appears determined to demonstrate its ability to strike ships before the US midterms that will decide control of Congress.
US fuel prices have surged by almost 70% since Trump launched his war on Iran, and the Republican party is bracing for punishment at the polls.

blocks.caption: US fuel prices have surged by almost 70% since Donald Trump launched his war on Iran. Photograph: Bizuayehu Tesfaye/Las Vegas Review-Journal/AP

blocks.text: According to two Iranian officials, Iran has recently begun using new tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions.
The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being ⁠to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said.
“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one of the two officials told Reuters.
The decision to adopt the new ​strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ‌ruling system, the officials added.

A US military official, ‌speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Tehran had changed tactics in one significant way. After the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, the IRGC had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to ‌identify potential targets, including American naval vessels, the official said.

Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the US official said.

articles.title: Container ship hit by projectile sinks in Strait of Hormuz, Singapore says
articles.summary: All 21 sailors on the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride were evacuated safely after it was hit by an projectile on Tuesday, maritime authorities say.

blocks.text: A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporean authorities.
All 21 crew members of GFS Pride were evacuated and no injuries were reported after the attack on Tuesday, which caused damage and a fire, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said.
Another Singapore-flagged container vessel, GFS Giselle, sustained hull damage after being hit by a projectile on Wednesday but was able to reach a safe anchorage with all 22 crew, it added.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines and sank while passing through what they called an "unauthorised" route in the Strait of Hormuz.

The Guards released photos that appeared to show a plume of black smoke rising from a container vessel that was still afloat but down by the stern. In other photos, dozens of containers and their contents could be seen floating in the water.
The Hydrographer of Pakistan warned mariners that GFS Pride had sunk 4 nautical miles (7.4km) north-west of Ras al-Sheikh Masud in Oman's Musandam Peninsula.

Meanwhile, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said that two unnamed container ships had reported being struck by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz between 16:40 and 17:00 GMT on Tuesday.
Both vessels sustained minor damage and were able to continue their passages, it added.

Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the Strait of Hormuz - which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea - and elsewhere in the Middle East since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.
At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 106 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization.
The Malta-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige, which was attacked near Oman on 4 March, is the only other vessel reported to have sunk in that time.

However, maritime risk management group Vanguard said on Wednesday that the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao was reported to be sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt, according to Reuters news agency.
One seafarer was killed when the Cape Dao's bridge and accommodation area were hit by an unknown projectile as it transited through the Strait of Hormuz, north-east of Khasab, Oman, on 23 September.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

Last month, crude exports through the waterway rose to around 80% of pre-war levels of 16 million barrels per day (bpd) on average, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler, despite an increase in attacks on shipping.

articles.title: Mont Blanc, the ‘roof of Europe’, loses more than a metre of height in a year
articles.summary:
Peak of French mountain now 4,807 metres high and fluctuates year by year due to changes in Alpine climate

Europe’s highest peak shrank by more than a metre last year, data has…

blocks.text: Europe’s highest peak shrank by more than a metre last year, data has shown.

Mont Blanc in France now stands 4,807.47 metres above sea level, a team of surveyors from the Haute-Savoie regional department said on Wednesday, putting “the roof of Europe” 1.29 metres lower than in 2025.

The mountain rock is about 4,792 metres tall but the summit constantly shifts as heat, wind and precipitation change the thickness of snow and ice on top. The height scientists recorded during an expedition last month is 1.88 metres greater than it was in 2023, when it reached the lowest levels in recent memory.

Chartered surveyors from the Union Nationale des Géomètres-Experts (UNGE) and the Ordre des Géomètres-Experts, who have regularly monitored the peak since 2001, used precise satellite technology to measure the mountain, and drones to create a detailed model of the snow and ice cap.

The summit has shrunk by 3.43 metres since a high of 4,810.90 metres in 2007, the data shows. The experts cautioned against linking fluctuations in height from year to year to the rapid loss of Alpine ice being caused by fossil fuel pollution.

“Regarding ice mass, it is essential to distinguish between changes in surface altitude and changes in the total volume or mass of ice,” a UNGE spokesperson said. “An increase in summit altitude does not necessarily mean that the mountain has gained ice mass, nor does it contradict the documented retreat of Alpine glaciers.”

Climate breakdown was a factor in western Europe’s hottest summer on record this year, scarring Alpine regions and melting ice at dizzying speed. Earlier this month, Swiss glaciologists warned of an “explosion of melt rates” after confirming that one-fifth of the country’s ice had been lost in the past five years, and 5.5% of volume was lost between 2025 and 2026.

Jean des Garets, the president of the Haute-Savoie departmental chamber of surveyors and the leader of the Mont Blanc expedition, said the warming trend can be seen with the naked eye in the rest of the Alpine massif but that “for the moment, climate change doesn’t seem to have the same impact above 4,000 metres”.

articles.title: Lacson refutes VP spokesperson's claim on impeachment costs
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo Lacson wants the spokesperson of Vice President Sara Duterte to correct his claims that the Senate spent P500 million for the impeachment trial, questioning how the latter even came…

blocks.text: Published October 14, 2026 11:30pm

Senator Panfilo Lacson wants the spokesperson of Vice President Sara Duterte to correct his claims that the Senate spent P500 million for the impeachment trial, questioning how the latter even came up with the number.

In a "24 Oras" report from Sandra Aguinaldo on Wednesday, Duterte’s spokesperson Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. said that 20 trial days were spent on the two articles of impeachment that were dropped, namely Articles I and IV.
"That is approximately P25 million in Senate operating cost per day, or P500 million of taxpayers' money, consumed on charges that will never be voted on,” Panelo said.

However, Lacson questioned where Panelo got this estimate. The national budget only allotted P27 million for the entire impeachment trial. Around P2 million of this was spent on robes and other expenses for the trial.

"The P25 million per day clearly refers to the legislative functions of the Senate, not to the impeachment trial as misinterpreted, and the basis was the Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE) and Personnel Services (PS) for one year, which I computed on a per-day basis when the Cayetano-led boycott resulted in zero-legislation output due to lack of quorum after his ouster as Senate President," Lacson said in a statement.
"I urge the VP's spokesman to rectify an obviously misleading figure of P500 million, as I assume it was an honest mistake on his part," he added.
In response, Panelo said that the expense was based on Senate President Win Gatchalian’s earlier estimate, which included expenses on salaries, electricity, utilities, and operating expenses.
Gatchalian later responded to Panelo’s claims in a statement, calling it untrue.

“That figure represents the cost of operating the entire Senate, including personnel and senators’ salaries, maintenance, rentals, and utilities. The Senate spends it with or without an impeachment trial,” Gatchalian said.

“The expenses directly attributable to the trial totaled P14,553,561.70 over 44 trial days, or an average of about P330,763 per day. These covered meals for personnel during extended sessions, supplies, overtime pay, and the rental of an outside venue for budget deliberations, as the trial occupied most of the Senate’s available rooms,” he added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: India urges Russia, Ukraine to protect Black Sea shipping
articles.summary: New Delhi wants Moscow and Kyiv to ensure safe commercial shipping in the Black Sea amid attacks that put Indian seafarers at risk.

image.caption: Attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Black Sea in recent months have highlighted the risks facing civilian crewsImage: UGC/AFP

blocks.text: India has urged both Russia and Ukraine to ensure safe passage for commercial shipping through the Black Sea, as attacks on merchant vessels put Indian seafarers at risk and threaten to disrupt vital food and energy supplies.
New Delhi says discussions with both sides are under way.

"The targeting of commercial shipping and seafarers in the region must end, and free and unimpeded navigation and commerce through the international waterways must be restored at the earliest," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said last week.

India accounts for more than 12% of the global seafaring workforce, with 311,936 maritime professionals, according to a 2026 industry report. And attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Black Sea in recent months have highlighted the risks facing civilian crews.

The Turkish-owned MV Royad Mammadov, a cargo ship carrying grain from Ukraine, caught fire and sank following an attack on Monday, killing two crew members. The three Indian nationals aboard the vessel survived, but sustained injuries and were taken to Romania to receive medical treatment.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia for launching the strike.
The Defense Ministry in Moscow separately said it had struck two Ukrainian cargo vessels in the Black Sea but did not specifically identify the ships.

The Liberian-flagged oil tanker Aframax Rio was also recently attacked by unmanned vessels off Russia's Black Sea coast near Sochi, according to Russian authorities. The vessel was carrying 23 Indians, but all of them were rescued.
How India has become Russia's trade lifeline
Can diplomacy deliver safety?

Anil Wadhwa, a former Indian diplomat, said India's proposal to halt attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea covered energy infrastructure, safe passage for grain and energy exports, and an end to strikes on merchant vessels.
"Securing an ironclad guarantee depends entirely on a broader cessation of hostilities between Russia and Ukraine in the maritime theater," Wadhwa told DW.
India's close relations with Russia and expanding engagement with Ukraine give New Delhi access to both sides, but do not guarantee either will honor a shipping arrangement.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has described India's proposal for a possible ceasefire with Russia as the "broadest" of the four offers Kyiv has received.
Russia has not publicly endorsed a binding safe-passage deal proposed by India, despite welcoming New Delhi's peace efforts.

Rajan Kumar of the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University said India could use its diplomatic leverage with Moscow to help bring the two sides towards an agreement.
"India could play a constructive role in facilitating dialogue between Russia and Ukraine, particularly on the issue of ensuring the safety of commercial shipping in the Black Sea," Kumar told DW.
How Ukraine fights in the Black Sea without a navy
Working with other powers to reach a deal
He argued that India should also work with other influential countries from the Global South, particularly China, Brazil and South Africa.

"A coordinated approach with these countries could enhance their collective diplomatic leverage and strengthen their capacity to persuade both parties to adopt mutually acceptable arrangements for maritime security," said Kumar.
India's initiative comes as US President Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend, although its scope and implementation mechanism remain unclear.

Harsh Pant, vice president of the New Delhi-based think tank Observer Research Foundation, said Trump's intervention could help India's efforts but might produce a narrower agreement that fails to address New Delhi's wider concerns.

"The energy ceasefire could be an initial confidence-building measure, whereas a Black Sea shipping arrangement requires additional commitments on attacks against merchant vessels, ports, maritime routes and the security of commercial traffic," Pant told DW.
"India need not compete with Washington for the public credit of mediation. It could instead press for the inclusion of broader maritime provisions in any US agreement,” he added.
Will India face a higher import bill?
Wadhwa said the proposed energy truce could also benefit Indian seafarers if it secured safe passage for energy cargoes.

"Although Ukraine alleges that the Russians have already breached this so-called truce, there will be pressure on both sides to allow energy cargoes safe passage. India is bound to gain as far as its crews are concerned in such a scenario," he said.
The disruption to Black Sea shipping also has other implications for India such as delays in shipments of key commodities and higher transport costs.

"A prolonged Black Sea disruption would elevate India's import bill mainly via higher freight on Russian crude and constrained soft oil supplies, with the strongest near-term transmission to domestic edible oil prices and food inflation," said Lekha Chakraborty, professor at the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy.

articles.title: Google partners with DepEd, CHED, TESDA to upskill teachers in AI
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Google Philippines launched the Google AI Educator Series (GES), a free bite-sized learning initiative for AI and Gemini training on October 13, 2026. The tech giant partnered…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Google Philippines launched the Google AI Educator Series (GES), a free bite-sized learning initiative for AI and Gemini training on October 13, 2026.

The tech giant partnered with the Department of Education (DepEd), the Commission on Higher Education (CHED), and the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) to reach public school teachers, government workers, and the general public.
GES timed its launch as October celebrates Teacher’s Month. Additionally, this also follows data that showed how more educators are looking to adapt AI into their curriculum.
The GES helps teachers understand the ethical use of AI, explore practical classroom applications, and follow prompt guidelines.
The scope of the partnership
DepEd will formally endorse GES nationwide through an upcoming joint curricular issuance.

This will include National Educators Academy of the Philippines (NEAP) accreditation to award Continuing Professional Development (CPD) credit units required for Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) license renewal.
GES, together with the government, aims to upskill over one million public school teachers in AI.
Next, CHED will issue an advisory for Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) that the GES is an optional resource to understand the AI tools for teaching, learning and research.
TESDA currently has GES embedded into the TESDA Online Program, a free e-learning platform.

“Building a future-ready nation starts with supporting our teachers. Our public school teachers carry a heavy workload every day, from crafting lesson plans to administrative reporting,” said DepEd Secretary Sonny Angara.

“Through our partnership with Google and the integration of the Google AI Educator Series into our enablement programs for teachers and staff, we are giving our teachers practical tools that lighten their administrative load. This allows them to spend less time on paperwork and more time doing what they do best: teaching and mentoring our learners.”
RELATED STORY: DOST explores Carabao mango as space food
Adapting learning to AI
A study presented by Google Philippines during the launch revealed that 86 percent of Filipino educators are inclined to use AI, but only 17 percent feel that they lack the training to do so.
Meanwhile, a UNESCO survey showed that 50 percent had low confidence or understanding of AI.
“Education is changing rapidly and AI is at the very center,” said Prep Palacios, Google Philippines Country Manager.
Google emphasized that although AI will soon become fully integrated into the curriculum, educators’ human touch remains more valuable.

“Amid all of this transformation, and the rise of AI, the soul of great teaching does not change, it will always be about human connection, empathy, and personal guidance. It cannot replace the heart of a teacher,” added Palacios.

articles.title: Germany's far-right AfD forges a pro-Russia alliance with the BSW
articles.summary: In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD and BSW are joining forces to push for negotiations with Moscow. What is driving this rapprochement?

image.caption: Following its landslide election win, the far-right AfD has placed itself at the center of the Saxony-Anhalt parliamentImage: dts-Agentur/picture alliance

blocks.text: The state parliament of the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt is calling for an immediate end to all German financial and military aid to Ukraine. The motion was passed during a special parliamentary session with the votes of the far-right populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing populist Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) which combines left-leaning economic positions with right-wing populist positions on immigration.

Both parties are urging Saxony-Anhalt's current state premier Sven Schulze of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), to advocate in the Bundesrat, Germany's upper house representing the federal states, for peace negotiations with Russia.
However, as the federal states have no specific powers in the field of foreign policy, the motion will have no direct impact on Germany's Ukraine policy.

Speaking on behalf of the BSW in the state parliament, legislator Claudia Wittig called on the premier to take action: "It is your responsibility to finally use every available avenue to work for peace."

The proposal drew sharp criticism from all other parties. "Anyone who demands a ceasefire only from the side that has been attacked is not calling for peace, but for capitulation," said CDU lawmaker Stefan Ruland.
What next after far-right AfD win in regional election?
AfD and BSW bonding over Russia

The special session took place against the backdrop of ongoing negotiations over the formation of a new state government in Saxony-Anhalt. The AfD had emerged as the clear winner of the September 2026 election, securing just under 44% of the vote. However, it fell short of an absolute majority in the state parliament and will need the support of other parties if it is to govern.

The BSW, which narrowly secured representation in the state parliament, is the only party willing to hold formal talks with the AfD on forming a government. Because the AfD is classified by the security authorities in the eastern German state as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" party, all other parties have ruled out any cooperation.
Observers view the joint motion by the AfD and BSW as a sign of closer and potentially enduring cooperation between two parties rooted in very different ideological traditions.

"Their common ground lies in their rejection of the political establishment, their pro-Putin stance, and their criticism of Germany's support for Ukraine," political scientist Armin Pfahl-Traughber of the University of Applied Administrative Sciences of the Federation said in an interview with DW.

The BSW was founded in 2024 as a breakaway from the socialist Left Party. Its founder, Sahra Wagenknecht, after whom the alliance was originally named, had long been a controversial figure on the German left and advocated far-reaching changes to Germany's economic policy. She was the Left Party's most prominent representative of the so-called "Communist Platform", which maintained close ties to Russia.

Over time, however, her socially conservative positions and criticism of Germany's immigration policy came under increasing scrutiny within the party. These growing tensions ultimately led to her departure from the Left Party and the founding of the BSW.

The AfD, too, has repeatedly expressed sympathy for Putin's system. Shortly after the start of Russia's war against Ukraine, Björn Höcke, the influential AfD state chairman in Thuringia, described Russia as a "champion of a world of free and sovereign states."
Historic parallels

The growing rapprochement between the two parties made headlines following a meeting in early October. At the invitation of a far-right publishing house, representatives of the AfD and BSW met in Saxony-Anhalt for what was described as a confidence-building dinner. Also in attendance were controversial figures from both the far right and the dogmatic left. According to their own accounts, participants from both sides explored the possibility of closer cooperation in a cordial atmosphere and in a spirit of mutual trust.
Far left? Far right? What is Germany's BSW?

Jürgen Elsässer, the host of the event and editor-in-chief of the right-wing magazine Compact, has for years promoted the idea of a so-called "cross-front" alliance (Querfront) between the far left and the far right in opposition to Germany's political establishment. He has long sought to build bridges between the two camps.

The historical model for this idea dates back to the 1930s, shortly before Adolf Hitler and the National Socialists came to power in Germany. At the time, national-conservative forces sought cooperation with elements of the political left in an effort to secure a majority of their own. As political scientist Armin Pfahl-Traughber explained in an interview with DW: "The aim, however, was not to save democracy from the National Socialists, but merely to establish an authoritarian political order without them." The idea failed. What followed were twelve years of terror under Nazi rule and World War II.

Pfahl-Traughber does not regard the cooperation between the AfD and BSW as a "cross-front" alliance: "I am not even sure that the BSW can still be classified as part of the political left." While the party's founder, Sahra Wagenknecht, has her roots on the left, she and her allies position themselves on the economic left but the cultural right, the political scientist argues.
AfD lawmaker elected speaker in Saxony-Anhalt
Are both AfD and BSW reactionary?

The prominent German historian and author Ilko-Sascha Kowalczuk likewise does not consider the BSW as a left-wing party. In an interview with DW, he argued: "The BSW was never left-wing; it was always reactionary."

Kowalczuk considers both the AfD and the BSW a threat to democracy: "The BSW and the AfD are two sides of the same coin. Both are mouthpieces for the Kremlin, both pursue similar domestic political objectives, and both seek a comparable anti-democratic transformation of the state into an authoritarian system."

Although the recent resolution passed by the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament is unlikely to have any immediate impact on Germany's policy towards Ukraine, Kowalczuk warns of its broader implications: "For now, the AfD and BSW remain isolated, but with positions like these they are appealing to large sections of society, particularly in eastern Germany. The erosion of solidarity with Ukraine will continue and will soon spread to larger segments of both the SPD and the CDU," he told DW.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Pope walking and recovering 'as expected' after surgery, doctors say
articles.summary: The 71-year-old Pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after the 90-minute procedure on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Watch: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer diagnosis
ByMaia Davies and Sarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondentReporting fromRome
Pope Leo XIV's recovery from surgery to remove a lower lobe of his lung is "progressing as expected", his doctors have said.
The 71-year-old pontiff has started to walk and has "resumed a normal diet" following the roughly 90-minute procedure, the medics said in an update shared by the Vatican.
The Pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.
Blood tests and an X-ray early on Wednesday showed his recovery was "proceeding normally", the doctors said, and he has also undergone respiratory physiotherapy.
The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.
"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before spending a "peaceful night" at the hospital.
The pontiff is expected to remain there for about a week as he recovers.

He had announced that he would be admitted for the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.

Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
A Vatican source told news agency AFP that further tests were carried out to see whether the cancer had spread.
The Vatican has stressed that the Pope, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness.
The news has shaken Catholics worldwide, many of whom will have recent memories of Pope Francis's hospital visits.
Pope Leo's predecessor, who died last year, also had part of his lung removed in his youth before suffering a series of respiratory infections later in life.
What is lung adenocarcinoma?
Adenocarcinomas develop in cells that produce mucus and are one of the most common types of lung cancer.

The long-term prognosis depends on a number of things, including the stage of the cancer when identified and the person's overall health. The earlier it is spotted, the better, and treatments have improved over the last few decades.
Some adenocarcinomas are picked up early - before symptoms develop - during routine tests. At later stages, lung cancer can cause a persistent cough, breathlessness, fatigue and weight loss.

articles.title: Albania: Fire at Education Ministry as students protest
articles.summary: Riot police deployed in the Albanian capital Tirana on the second day of student protests. The sudden outbreak seemed at least somewhat reminiscent of the widespread demos in France courting…

image.caption: Riot police and water cannons deployed in the captial TiranaImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS

blocks.text: Albania's Education Ministry caught fire on Wednesday in a second day of student protests over corruption and education.
The scenes were at least somewhat reminiscent of the protracted student demonstrations in France in recent weeks.

They are probably the most violent outburst of low-level anti-corruption protests against Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and the main opposition led by Sali Barisha that started in May this year.

blocks.caption: Many of the demonstrators wore face coveringsImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS

blocks.text: What happened in Tirana's student protests?
Police deployed riot police and used tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds in the capital Tirana.

Thousands of protesters gathered in front of the Education Ministry on Wednesday, many obscuring their faces. Some threw bricks at the building, damaged barriers on the sidewalks and overturned trash cans.
A bank near the Education Ministry also caught fire, according to the Reuters news agency citing a witness.
The demonstration started on Tuesday with a peaceful gathering of several hundred people outside the Education Ministry but quickly escalated and turned violent in places.
Police early on Wednesday reported around 40 detentions and 13 people injured, including six police officers. Unrest continued long after these figures were issued.

blocks.caption: Police used tear gas and water cannons on demonstrators in parts of TiranaImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS

blocks.text: Government says demonstrations degenerated into 'orchestrated violence'
Deputy Prime Minster Albana Kociu posted a video of demonstrations on Facebook saying it was "disheartening to see the culture of protest degenerate into orchestrated violence."

She said that the attacks on institutions and police and the "senseless destruction of public property" were "not the language through which the youth should express themselves." Instead, she said they were reminiscent of the "old habits of those who use young people to mask their own political incompetence."
In another post, Kociu called on students who believe in the right to protest to "distance" themselves from "violence and vandalism."
Student organizers say the protests revolve around conditions at universities, higher education costs, financial support and employment prospects after graduation.

More generally, Albania has faced a series of demonstrations this year sometimes referred to as the "Flamingo Revolution." These were at least partly prompted by a controversial construction project on the Adriatic Coast in a protected area where flamingos live.

But these partly environmental protests have also had a more general theme of dissatisfaction with Albania's dominant political forces. PM Edi Rama's Socialists and Sali Barisha's right-wing democrats have alternated in government for more than 30 years, ever since the post-Cold War democratic transition in the former communist country.
Albania: Europe's new billionaire playground

The timing is also conspicuous, with the demonstrations starting amid prominent international coverage of widespread school and student protests in France in recent weeks leading to similarly restless scenes.

articles.title: Robot controlled by 2 men gropes teen girl in Germany. Police call it 'new territory'
articles.summary: German authorities opened an investigation into possible sexual harassment after a robot controlled by two young men touched the buttocks of a 16-year-old girl and made thrusting movements toward…

image.caption: This photo provided by Cologne police on Oct. 11, 2026, shows a robot that was seized as evidence. (Cologne Police/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

German authorities opened an investigation into possible sexual harassment after a robot controlled by two young men touched the buttocks of a 16-year-old girl and made thrusting movements toward her, police said.
Robot's owner, 16, and friend, 19, reportedly filmed alleged assault

Police in the western city of Cologne responded after the incident overnight Saturday to Sunday in which the robot’s suspected 16-year-old owner and a 19-year-old companion were said to have filmed the alleged assault.
They were said to have streamed the incident and commentated on it online.

Cologne police spokesman Christoph Bermel said the two male teenagers have not been charged but are considered suspects, and investigators were examining whether the robot’s movements were pre-programmed or controlled in real time.
Police were unfamiliar with this type of incident, he said.
"We have not been aware of this phenomenon so far," Bermel told The Associated Press, saying it was "new territory for us."

blocks.text: Emergency teams that were dispatched to the scene near a fast-food restaurant found the robot in the trunk of a vehicle, Cologne police said in a statement on Monday. The robot and the two young men’s mobile phones were confiscated.
North Rhine Westphalia Police Cologne, on Facebook, posted an image of the red-and-gold robot lying on the ground.
The robot, said to be almost four feet tall, was dressed in a white tank top, black sweatpants and wearing a gold chain and sunglasses. It also had what appears to be a fake moustache.

Videos circulated on the internet show two young men escorting the robot toward a group of women, bumping into one and hugging others, on a lively nighttime street. One of the men repeatedly shouts at the robot and pulls it backward after it makes sexual gestures, prompting laughter among people in the area.
On the police’s Facebook account on Tuesday, officers criticized inappropriate comments and warned that sharing or joking about such incidents can worsen the impact on any victim.

articles.title: France’s students are angry about more than crumbling classrooms and missing teachers
articles.summary:
Beneath a wave of school protests in France lies a more existential worry: the future prospects of an entire generation

•

blocks.text: Say what you will about France’s high schools, they still produce world-class slogan writers. Here’s a brief selection spotted during three weeks of blockades and marches over chronic teacher shortages, overcrowded classes and crumbling buildings:

“Pas d’avenir, pas de calme” (No future, no calm). “Diplômés aujourd’hui, précaires demain” (Graduates today, insecure tomorrow). “Vous détruisez notre futur, on bloque votre présent” (You destroy our future, we block your present).

A couple more: “Nos lycées tombent en ruines, comme nos espoirs” (Our schools, like our hopes, are falling into ruin”). “On n’est pas mal éduqués, on n’est pas écoutés” (We’re not badly brought up, we’re just not being listened to).

Spot the common theme? The protests, which continued this week with more than 160,000 on the streets on Tuesday, might be over very material problems – but beneath them there clearly lies an altogether more existential worry.

This generation fears its future will be one of diminishing prospects, poorly paid, unstable jobs, unaffordable living costs and steadily decaying public infrastructure – the end, in short, of the basic socioeconomic security their parents, mostly, enjoyed.

That was the central theme of a 30-second Instagram post I recorded last week with the Guardian’s social media team and that, at time of writing, had been watched almost 540,000 times – with young people in France the largest single group of viewers.

The same core concerns underlie youth protests elsewhere – notably, ongoing mass housing demonstrations in Spain, where the twentysomethings of Madrid and Barcelona are in revolt at the monthly rental on a one-bed flat costing an entire monthly median salary.

In France, teenagers in Seine-Saint-Denis, a low-income area in the north of Paris, show reporters pictures of broken chairs and desks, holes in walls, leaking ceilings, mould, shattered toilets and defective audiovisual equipment. Some have gone months without key teachers.
The consequence, here, is protest.

As Kitty Sayers, who went to school in France, explained, France’s republic “was born of insurrection and has never forgotten it … The language of rights, citizenship and collective power is woven into French education.”

This means that in French schools protest is “taught as a legally framed, fundamental right and a civic responsibility”. But the government’s response has also been arguably very French: riot police, teargas, baton charges and stun grenades.

More than 250 pupils have been injured, along with about 100 school staff and 750 police. One teen has lost a hand from a stun grenade, another the sight in one eye, a third his teeth. More than 6,000 people – almost all minors – have been detained.

After a public outcry, the interior minister last week suspended the use of stun grenades. But as Alexander Hurst observed, when pupils complain about the state of their schools “and the response is riot police, the government has lost the plot”.
Wider public support

blocks.caption: ‘Hands off our children’ … there is widespread support for the protests.  Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters

blocks.text: If the government hoped public opinion would be on its side, it miscalculated. Teachers’ and other unions, parents and university students have marched with the pupils, and a poll this week showed 57% of the public approved of the protests, with 33% opposed.

They come at a particularly delicate time for France’s political establishment. Presidential elections to replace Emmanuel Macron are due next spring, and without a parliamentary majority his government is caught in legislative deadlock.

Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally and the radical-left La France Insoumise of Jean-Luc Mélenchon are weaponising the protests, the former castigating an out-of-control youth, the latter an out-of-control police, and both blaming centrist incompetence.
after newsletter promotion

Above all, the government’s financial room for manoeuvre is all but nonexistent. As Philip Inman pointed out, with a debt-to-GDP ratio and a budget deficit both among the highest in the EU, France has no cash to spare – and the markets are watching.

So while cost-cutting will only provoke more unrest, the absence of it could trigger a boycott of French bonds, or even a default and bailout (although as the economist Paul Krugman says, France “may have crossed from too big to fail to too big to save”).

Ultimately, there seems little doubt France will have to make some of the same painful adjustments to bring its debt back under control that Italy, Spain and Greece made a decade or more ago – and to which French public reaction could be dramatic.

We began with slogans; let’s end with some. The best-known French youth protest – a revolution, more or less – was, of course, May 1968. Comparing its iconic posters with those of today’s demonstrating school pupils is instructive.

In 1968, there was “Sous les pavés, la plage” (Beneath the cobblestones, the beach); “L’imagination au pouvoir” (Put imagination in charge); “L’ennui est contre-révolutionnaire” (Boredom is counter-revolutionary).

Those, you can see, were slogans born out of infinite possibility: a generation that, in overthrowing the old social hierarchies, never doubted its material survival. May 68 was about blowing open the doors of a rigid, outmoded society to grasp a bright future.
Today’s students are fighting to stop the doors slamming shut on them altogether.
Guardian live-streamed event – Hacking Tech

blocks.caption: Naomi Klein, one of the featured speakers at Hacking Tech. Photograph: Sebastian Nevols/The Guardian

blocks.text: Big tech and AI pose immense challenges for our societies and democracies. The Guardian is partnering with French news investigative outlet Mediapart, on a live event called Hacking Tech in Paris at 1pm CEST on Saturday 17 October. Speakers include Naomi Klein, Emily M Bender, Paris Marx, Sönke Iwersen and the Guardian’s UK technology editor, Rob Booth.
The event is free and open to the public but don’t worry if you can’t be there: the debates will be live-streamed without a paywall on Mediapart’s YouTube channel. Tune in!

articles.title: Climate change and drone attacks exacerbate the humanitarian crisis in war-torn Sudan
articles.summary: Aid groups warn of an imminent collapse of the health system as fighting continues to displace civilians amid the planting season. The UN has extended an arms embargo, but only for Darfur.

image.caption: Aid organizations warn of an imminent collapse of Sudan's health system amid funding shortagesImage: AFP

blocks.text: In Sudan, clashes between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have intensified in North Kordofan and parts of Blue Nile state. The fighting has forced thousands of civilians to flee amid the planting season.
Since war broke out between the two factions and their allied militias in April 2023, both sides have fought for power. However, neither has managed to establish control over the entire country.

The SAF, the nation's official army, is in control of Sudan's north and center, including the capital, Khartoum, while the RSF maintains its presence in the western Darfur region and parts of the south.

The brutal war has plunged Sudan into one of the world's worst humanitarian and displacement crises, according to the United Nations and international aid organizations. The estimated death toll ranges from 40,000 to 250,000 people as reliable figures remain difficult to obtain amid the ongoing fighting. More than 12.4 million Sudanese have also been displaced, both within Sudan and to neighboring countries.

blocks.caption: Fighting between the RSF and SAF is prompting thousands of civilians to flee from their homes amid the planting seasonImage: Faiz Abubakr/Middle East Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: This week, the aid organization Action Against Hunger sounded the alarm.
"24.6 million people are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity," Jan Sebastian Friedrich-Rust, executive director of the German section of the NGO, told DW.

Friedrich-Rust added that an estimated 825,000 children younger than 5 suffer from severe acute malnutrition in 2026, while a total of 4.2 million children and pregnant or breastfeeding women are thought to be acutely malnourished.

In October, the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) — which monitors food insecurity and uses the internationally recognized Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) system — also warned that several areas including camps for internally displaced people in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan, are expected to face Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5), the most severe classification of acute food insecurity.

"The situation in Sudan continues to deteriorate and humanitarian needs are growing, even as the resources to respond are shrinking," Fabrizia Falcione, the Sudan representative of the United Nations Population Fund, the UN agency for sexual and reproductive health, said.

"I recently visited the displacement camp Tawila and I am still struggling to find the words to describe what I witnessed," Falcione told DW. "Imagine a population larger than that of Frankfurt, Germany, forced to flee their homes and seek refuge in one place in less than three years."
She added that more than 700,000 people there rely on just one hospital capable of performing Caesarean sections.

Despite repeated warnings about the deteriorating humanitarian situation, the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, which calls for $2.9 billion (€2.59 bn), is just 41% funded, with $1.2 billion (€1.07 bn) received from international donors so far.
Community kitchen fights hunger in Sudan's Tawila camp
Climate shocks exacerbate Sudan's humanitarian crisis
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) recently warned that extreme heat and heavy flooding are worsening the crisis in Sudan.

"This year, a massive heatwave brought power cuts of up to 12 hours per day in some regions," Hager Ali, a Sudan researcher at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies (GIGA), told DW. "Riverbeds and dried-out fields are barren, which comes on top of the damage from combat, the RSF's scorched-earth tactics and environmental destruction."
While the drought is affecting roughly half the country, heavy rains and localized flooding have worsened conditions in other areas of Sudan.
"As if that wasn't enough, there is also a massive shortage of fertilizer and diesel," Ali told DW.

Sudan relies on imported fertilizer and diesel shipped from the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. However, amid the wider Iran war, Iran has been blocking shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, while the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen have threatened and at times disrupted shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
"Fertilizer supply collapsed from 450,000 metric tons to only about 50,000" in 2026, Ali said, adding that a similar diesel shortage and the soaring cost of diesel compound the situation in two ways.
"Agricultural equipment uses diesel and the transportation of humanitarian and agricultural goods within the country is getting a lot more expensive," Ali said.
In October, the International Food Policy Research Institute warned that staple food- and fuel prices in Sudan rose sharply in September 2026.

blocks.caption: Al-Harith Idriss Al-Harith Mohamed, Sudan's permanent representative  to the United Nations, opposed an extension of the arms embargo across Sudan, citing disadvantages for the Sudanese Armed Forces Image: Luiz Rampelotto/EuropaNewswire/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Limited arms embargo curbs hope for an end to the war

Observers have long pointed out that the war in Sudan will not end until foreign backers stop supplying arms. The SAF is officially supported by Egypt, Turkey, Russia and Iran while the United Arab Emirates is alleged to be the RSF's main backer, a claim Abu Dhabi denies.
However, in October, the UN Security Council extended the existing arms embargo only on Sudan's Darfur region until December 11, dropping calls for a nationwide embargo.

"To expand the UN embargo across Sudan would have included drones in particular," Hager Ali said, noting that Sudan is one of the biggest theaters for drone warfare: As of 2026, the leading cause of civilian casualties in Sudan are drone strikes.

She also told DW that Al-Harith Idriss al-Harith Mohamed, Sudan's permanent representative to the United Nations, opposed the extention of the embargo over concerns that it would disproportionately limit the Sudanese Armed Forces on the battlefield.

"An arms embargo would deter potential backers from cooperating with the Sudanese Armed Forces, whereas the Rapid Support Forces don't necessarily source their weapons through official ways," Hager Ali said.

"The RSF rely on trafficking with other militias, private military contractors and traders in the region," she said, adding that because the RSF obtains supplies from numerous sources and actors, it is difficult to target the group through a single embargo.

articles.title: DOST explores Carabao mango as space food
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Science and Technology–Philippine Nuclear Research Institute (DOST-PNRI) is exploring how to develop Carabao mango into food for long-duration space missions.…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Science and Technology–Philippine Nuclear Research Institute (DOST-PNRI) is exploring how to develop Carabao mango into food for long-duration space missions.
The project is set to be featured at the National Science, Technology, and Innovation Week (NSTW) on November 25 to 29, 2026, in General Santos City, South Cotabato.

The Philippine Space Mango Program brings together DOST-PNRI, the University of the Philippines Diliman for food science expertise, the Philippine Space Agency, and the Batangas Mango High Value Growers Agriculture Cooperative (BAMAHGACO) as a partner in mango production.
RELATED STORY: New HVAC training center opens as El Niño raises the stakes for cooling efficiency
A taste of home in space

“We’re taking the Carabao mango and exploring how it can be part of the Filipino story in space,” said Gina B. Abrera of DOST-PNRI, the program’s project leader in a press release. “We want a product that can travel far, represent our identity, and remind future astronauts of home.”
Beyond its nutritional value, the project aims to give future Filipino astronauts a familiar taste of home as the country works toward sending its first astronaut to space by 2035.
“We’re not just thinking about nutrition. We’re thinking about identity, comfort, and home,” Abrera added.
Potential applications on Earth

Aside from its potential use in space missions, the project is also expected to help strengthen the Philippine dried mango industry’s competitiveness in international markets and explore food solutions for emergencies and disaster response.

NSTW is DOST’s annual celebration of the country’s scientific and technological achievements, bringing together researchers, industry representatives, government agencies, and academic institutions to showcase homegrown innovations.
