articles.title: Iran: Political infighting deepens as economic woes mount during war
articles.summary: Hardliners are stepping up pressure on Iran's government and calling for Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi's removal. The oil minister resigned, but that's doing little to ease the pressure on…

image.caption: Hardliners in Iran's parliament want Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi goneImage: Hadi Mizban/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Hardliners are piling the pressure on Iran’s government and calling for the removal of Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad’s resignation is also failing to ease the pressure on President Masoud Pezeshkian.
As the war continues and diplomatic efforts to find a solution make little headway, the internal power struggle is intensifying. President Pezeshkian’s government is the focus of mounting tension.

Hardliners in Iran's parliament are pushing for impeachment proceedings against Araghchi. A trigger for the discontent was Araghchi's meeting with US negotiators on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Critics accuse the foreign minister of holding the talks without official authorization.

blocks.caption: Iran's oil exports have plunged as a result of the US blockade of the Strait of HormuzImage: Asghar Besharati/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In a letter, Tehran lawmaker Amirhossein Sabeti informed parliamentary speaker Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf that he had registered a motion to impeach Araghchi on parliament’s online portal. Lawmaker Hossein-Ali Haji-Deligani also said parliament could use its oversight powers, including impeachment proceedings.
A structural problem within Iran’s power system

"When the regime is forced to negotiate, as it is in the current situation and in talks with the United States, the supreme leader or the hardline core of power avoids taking responsibility and shifts it onto elected institutions and moderate forces within the government," political analyst Ali Afshari, who lives in the United States, told DW.
Hardliners can use this approach to attack moderate factions over decisions that were previously agreed upon within the power apparatus, Afshari said.
He added that hardliners serve an important function within the Islamic Republic.

"The role of hardliners in the Islamic Republic is to influence public opinion, the political system's traditional supporters and the values of the Islamic Republic in both domestic and foreign policy," he said.
All the Ayatollah's men — ensuring the regime's survival

Hardliners held a parliamentary majority during the implementation of the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), the 2015 nuclear deal, and voiced their political opposition. Their resistance, however, ultimately did not affect the signing of the agreement.
"The Foreign Ministry is not a decision-maker. It implements what the government asks of it — and Araghchi is operating within that framework," Afshari said.
Lawmakers must first collect a set number of signatures to move forward with impeachment proceedings.
The lucrative business of oil

The timing of the latest move is significant: Iran's government finds itself under enormous economic pressure. Meanwhile, oil exports, which are one of the country's key sources of revenue, have fallen sharply as a result of the US blockade.
The resignation of Oil Minister Paknejad adds to the pressure. Officially, he stepped down for personal reasons.

Umud Shokri, an energy strategist, geopolitical analyst and energy security expert, casts doubt that a change at the helm of the Oil Ministry would alter the situation. Iran relies on networks that enable it to export oil despite sanctions, Shokri said. Opaque structures have become entrenched, making it harder for the government to control key revenue streams.
Circumventing sanctions has become a lucrative business for certain factions within Iran's political system, he said.
"By law, these revenues should be under state control. But we know that has not been the case for years," Shokri said.
Economic opacity has deepened during the sanctions period, he added, under the pretext of national security and protecting the population.
Fighting Iran war, can US military sustain a long conflict?

Private actors with close ties to the country's centers of power, particularly the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), have developed methods to sell oil to the armed forces through hidden channels. Neither the prices nor the commissions charged or the total sums involved are transparent.
"The government has only limited influence over these transactions. The Revolutionary Guards, in particular, would organize and control such deals," Shokri said.
Analysts have signaled that political and economic situation could likely deteriorate further in the coming days and weeks.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Leaders of India’s Cockroach party jailed for violating ban on protest site
articles.summary:
Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das will spend spend five days in prison for entering Delhi’s Jantar Mantar – a historic protest site that has been closed by authorities

Two leaders of India’s…

blocks.text: Two leaders of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement have been sent to jail for five days for violating a ban on protests at a site in central Delhi.

A court ordered that Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, leaders of the Cockroach Janata party (CJP) movement, spend five days in Delhi’s Tihar prison for jumping over police barricades, holding up slogans and waving the Indian flag at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar.

CJP leaders said the action was taken to demonstrate against the brutal crackdown on youth protesters in Delhi over the weekend and the decision by the Delhi police to shut-down Jantar Mantar – a stretch of road surrounding an observatory in central Delhi – as the capital’s designated protest site, a status it has held for more than 30 years.

“You cannot denotify the resistance,” said Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the CJP, in a social media post which showed three of his fellow leaders entering Jantar Mantar, before they were tackled and detained by police on Tuesday.

On Saturday, the CJP – a movement with a substantial following among India’s youth – called for a protest in Jantar Mantar to demand the resignation of the election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing the mass disenfranchisement of millions of Indian voters.

The CJP, alongside the opposition political parties and student groups, have accused Kumar of revising India’s electoral roll to advantage the ruling Narendra Modi government, a charge his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) denies.

blocks.caption: Delhi police inspect vehicles near the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi on Tuesday. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The election commission has ​denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters ‌can re-enrol.

Police denied permission for the protest on Saturday to take place and instead imposed a sweeping security crackdown. About 30,000 police and paramilitary were deployed to prevent the demonstration in Jantar Mantar, which was blocked with barricades. More than 7,000 people were detained.

In the aftermath, the police declared that protests would no longer be allowed at Jantar Mantar, provoking outrage among the CJP leaders. Prior to his arrest, Das posted: “Why is Narendra Modi scared of Jantar Mantar? Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India.”
Ranka and Das ‌were among about a dozen people who jumped the barricades on Tuesday to enter the grounds of the Jantar Mantar to wave flags and chant slogans.
In response to their sentencing, CJP founder Dipke accused the Modi government of resorting to “cowardly tactics” to “crush dissent”.

The response by the Modi government to the protests that have erupted nationwide – including the mass detentions – has drawn criticism from the UN human rights commissioner and human rights groups such as Amnesty.
The Indian government hit back at the UN statement on the protests, calling it an “unwarranted and constitute an unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of the country”.
It was also met with concern by a UK political delegation visiting Delhi, led by trade minister Jonny Reynolds who confirmed he had raised it with the Indian government.
Kiran Stacey contributed reporting

articles.title: World's oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
articles.summary: Archaeologists say the wreck is up to 4,700 years old, dating to the Early Bronze Age.
articles.byline: Alison Francis, Rebecca Morelle, Kevin Church

blocks.text: Artefacts from the ship were found just off the coast of Kekova Island
ByAlison FrancisRebecca Morelle and Kevin ChurchBBC News Science
The world's oldest shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists say.
They have dated it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old, which is the Early Bronze Age, and is around the same time that the Great Pyramid was being built.
The ship's wooden structure has not survived, but the ceramic storage pots it was carrying were lying on the sea floor and, remarkably, some still contain traces of what they held inside.
The archaeologists who found the ship say it was about 10m in length and was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea.
"The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," said Prof Hakan Öniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The divers found three stone anchors, as ships carried spares on long voyages

blocks.text: Image source, Hakan Öniz
The divers found three stone anchors, as ships carried spares on long voyages
The wreck is close to the shore of Kekova Island in Antalya, Turkey. The artefacts lie scattered across an underwater slope, just 30m beneath the waves.
Three large stone anchors were found, as well as more than 30 ceramic storage pots, called amphorae.
The fact that none of the ship's wood remained meant techniques like radiocarbon dating - which measures a form of carbon in organic materials - could not be used to determine its age.
Instead, archaeologists analysed the shape of the amphorae. Because pottery styles have changed over time, different styles are linked to particular periods.
The Kekova ceramics are distinctive, with two handles, a ridge in the middle and a flat base.
Öniz said this design matched other amphorae unearthed in Egypt and the Middle East that were known to be 4,400-4,700 years old.
"Comparing the decoration techniques… we can definitely say our wreck is Early Bronze Age. This is 100%."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The amphorae were recovered and taken on board the research ship

blocks.text: The amphorae were recovered and taken on board the research ship

blocks.caption: Image caption, After thousands of years underwater, the fragile artefacts are now being carefully conserved

blocks.text: After thousands of years underwater, the fragile artefacts are now being carefully conserved
Divers from the expedition brought the pots up to the surface, where they are now being carefully conserved after so many thousands of years underwater.

Dr Karin Sowada, an archaeologist from Macquarie University, Australia, examined the amphorae after they were recovered. Some were intact and she was surprised to see they still contained a viscous, glossy residue.
"I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots…. a lot of this material was still remaining," she said.
The team is now working to find out exactly what was being carried in the amphorae.
"It could be olive oil, it could be wine, it could be tree resins," Sowada said.

"It's possible that [the residue] could actually be the result of reuse of the jars. I mean, these jars are huge - they're not things that you just ship away and then never see again. People would have emptied these jars on arrival and potentially used them for many, many, many years."

blocks.caption: Map graphic showing Europe, Middle East and Africa. The start of the voyage is labelled on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea, Kekova Island is labelled - it is on the south coast of Turkey, Troy is labelled, which is in northwest Turkey and Crete in southern Greece. The indicates a possible rout…

blocks.text: The wreck and its cargo are also shedding light on trade in the ancient world.
The archaeologists say the ship started its voyage from somewhere along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean.
They believe it was taking goods to either the ancient city of Troy, in what is now north-western Turkey, or to the Minoan people in Crete.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The divers worked underwater to carefully excavate the artefacts

blocks.text: The divers worked underwater to carefully excavate the artefacts
Travelling by sea was fraught with danger, particularly around Kekova Island, where the strong currents and winds have claimed many ships.
There are hundreds of wrecks in the area, and the Mediterranean Archaeology Association specialises in finding and studying them.
Öniz says that when he is diving on the wreck his first thoughts are about the lives of the people who were connected to this vessel.
"We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years.

"We are always thinking of the sailors... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back."

The shipwreck is owned by the Turkish Ministry of Culture. Its minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said the artefacts that have been recovered would be put on display in the new Mediterranean Underwater Archaeology Museum in Antalya when it opens in the coming months.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The depth meant the divers could only spend 30 minutes at a time exploring it

blocks.text: The depth meant the divers could only spend 30 minutes at a time exploring it
The Kekova discovery now tops the list of the world's oldest shipwrecks.
Previously, the record holder was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, an island in southern Greece, which dates to about 4,200 years ago.
The oldest known intact shipwreck, where the wood is still preserved, was found in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria. It dates to about 2,400 years ago.

articles.title: Iranian woman handed death sentence for ‘blasphemy’ in social media post
articles.summary:
Rights groups warn of Tehran regime’s increasing use of executions to suppress dissent, with at least 600 this year

Human rights groups have raised the alarm over the growing number of death…

blocks.text: Human rights groups have raised the alarm over the growing number of death sentences and executions in Iran, after reports that a 23-year-old woman, Najmeh Amini, has been sentenced to death for blasphemy over a social-media post.

Amini, an accounting student, is being held in Vakilabad prison in the north-east city of Mashhad. She has been sentenced to more than 12 years in prison and death in separate cases heard by a revolutionary and a criminal court.
A source close to Amini’s family told the US-based Human Rights Activists in Iran (HRAI) that Amini was sentenced to death on charges of “sab ol-nabi” (insulting the prophet).
In the second case, Amini was sentenced to 12 years, six months and one day on charges including acting against national security and spreading propaganda against the regime.

Amini was arrested by security forces during January’s nationwide protests, which were suppressed with a deadly crackdown. Thousands were reported killed, while the HRAI news agency, Hrana, said more than 50,000 people were arrested.
In an audio recording released from the prison last month, Amini appealed for international intervention, calling on the UN, lawyers and rights groups to investigate her case.
“I do not want to make a hero out of myself today. I only want one thing: be my voice,” she said.

“I am an innocent young girl with so many hopes and dreams,” Amini said. “I have parents who are waiting for me. A family that every night, with the fear of losing me, turns their night into morning.”

Rights groups warn that the Iranian authorities are increasingly using capital punishment to instil fear and suppress dissent. According to the Oslo-based Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), more than 600 executions have already been carried out this year.

blocks.caption: Iranians block a Tehran street during nationwide protests in January, which were sparked by the weak economy but became political and anti-regime.  Photograph: Mahsa/Middle East Images/AFP

blocks.text: Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of IHRNGO, said Amini’s case should be seen as a serious warning.

“Sentencing a young woman to death for what she posted on social media risks normalising the use of the death penalty against peaceful expression and pushing the boundaries of the death penalty even further,” he said.

Amiry-Moghaddam added that the Iranian authorities were testing the international community’s “tolerance” towards capital punishment. “If the international community does not respond firmly now, cases like this could become far more common,” he said.

Under article 262 of Iran’s Islamic penal code, insulting the prophet Muhammad or revered Shia figures is punishable by death. However, article 263 provides exemptions for statements made while intoxicated or without deliberate intent, although offenders may still face up to 74 lashes in certain circumstances.

According to the Iranian newspaper Khorasan, which confirmed the judicial proceedings, Amini told the court she had posted the remarks while hallucinating after taking psychedelic mushrooms with friends and her defence argued it was a “slip of the tongue”.
The presiding judge rejected her defence, reportedly asking: “Why, in that same hallucinatory state, did you not insult other individuals or opponents of the regime, such as America and Israel?”
Amini’s death sentence is not final and remains subject to appeal before Iran’s supreme court.
The student’s sentencing comes at a time when Iranian lawmakers are seeking to criminalise contact with all foreign media, including posts on social media deemed to be financed by another country.
Elnaz*, 24, who took part in the protests in Tehran in January and was arrested over social-media posts at the height of the war in March, said she lived in constant fear of surveillance.

“I was arrested even though my social-media account was private. So it’s not just the regime’s cyber-police we have to worry about. There’s also this constant mistrust, this feeling that someone is watching me all the time, even when I’m alone in my room.
“I’m scared to post anything on social media … but after everything they’ve put us through, do we really have anything left to lose? They can kill us even if we don’t post anything on social media.”

Although executions in Iran have surged in recent years, reaching their highest level in three decades, death sentences for blasphemy remain relatively rare. The last documented case was on 8 May 2023, when Yousef Mehrad and Sadrollah Fazeli-Zare were executed after being convicted of blasphemy-related offences tied to social-media activity.
* Name has been changed to protect her identity

articles.title: ’How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?’ Why Indian voters are on the streets
articles.summary:
Anger at electoral roll changes has boiled over, sparking a crisis for Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government

Born into a small village in West Bengal, Shahida Fakir had always taken…
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Shaikh Azizur Rahman

blocks.text: Born into a small village in West Bengal, Shahida Fakir had always taken her vote for granted. That was, until it was suddenly taken away. She presented officials with her Indian birth certificate and family land documents from the village going back to 1962.
Both her parents had been on the electoral roll going back decades, so she showed proof of that too. But when the final revised voter list came out in April, Fakir was not on it.

The 38-year-old migrant worker, born into a poor Muslim family, was not alone. Since last year, 130 million names – more than the population of Japan – have been removed from India’s electoral roll through a process known as SIR, or special intensive revision. In the nearly eight decades since India’s independence, never have the voter rolls shrunk by such a huge amount over such a short time.

blocks.caption: Shahida Fakir is staying in a village in Bangladesh after she was detained on suspicion of being an illegal immigrant and pushed across the border. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: The Narendra Modi government has called SIR a legitimate exercise to clean up the electoral rolls. Overseen by the election commission, tens of millions of dead and duplicate names have been removed. Yet so have the names of millions of living Indian citizens.

Critics allege that the pledge to “purify” India’s voter roll of illegal immigrants has instead been used for more sinister purposes – disenfranchising tens of millions of Muslims, other minorities, and poor and lower caste communities, who are largely not BJP voters.

In a matter of weeks, nationwide anger at SIR has boiled up and spilled out on to the streets of India’s biggest cities, presenting a formidable challenge to the government. Over the weekend, Delhi was transformed into a high-security fortress of barricades, roadblocks and tens of thousands of police and paramilitaries who detained thousands of people, as they attempted to stop youth-led protests calling for the man who oversaw SIR, the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down immediately.

On Monday, opposition parties – who have decried SIR as a “weapon for vote theft” by the Modi government – drew tens of thousands of supporters as they marched through the capital and presented a petition to the supreme court, demanding Kumar’s resignation. The youth-led Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, who were behind the call for Saturday’s action, have vowed to “fight on” in their protests against SIR.

Opposition and civil society leaders allege that SIR has already given the BJP an electoral advantage in states such as Bihar and West Bengal, claims the party denied. Others say the exercise has had even more concerning implications: under changes to SIR unilaterally implemented by Kumar, the election commission has become the arbiter of Indian citizenship, a sweeping overreach of its remit.

The consequences are already playing out in West Bengal, where Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) recently came to power and began a crackdown on “illegal” immigrants, complete with several new detention centres. Civil society groups say Muslims excluded by SIR are being targeted.

Fakir was among them. Just three months after the voter list was published – and while her hearing to challenge her exclusion was pending – she was picked up by police and accused of being an illegal Bangladeshi immigrant.

In July she was pushed over the border to Bangladesh, a country she had never been to nor had any connection with, and remains stuck there. “I have all the documents to prove I am an Indian citizen,” she said in a tearful phone call from the Bangladesh border village where she has been sheltering. “I fell on their feet and begged the police not to send me to Bangladesh but they pushed me over the border.”

blocks.caption: A protest march in Dhaka, Bangladesh, against India’s ‘push-ins’ of Muslims at the border in June. Photograph: Mamunur Rashid/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: A Bangladesh border guard officer confirmed Fakir’s account. “We checked all her documents and are convinced that she is an Indian citizen,” they said. In September, her family submitted a petition to the supreme court challenging her deportation. The Indian government was given a month to respond.

“All I want is to return to my family and my home in India. I am waiting desperately for that day,” she said. The backlog of millions of voters in West Bengal challenging their exclusion means it could be years before Fakir’s case is heard.

Those across West Bengal who have been stripped of their votes speak of their terror of being accused of being an alien in their own land. Some have had benefits taken away. Mohammad Hedayet Ullah Siddiqui, 80, from the North 24 Parganas district, said his grandfather had been a freedom fighter for Indian independence and three generations of his family were on the voter rolls. Yet after SIR, Siddiqui described his “humiliation” on finding his name gone.

“With my name erased from the voter list, I am in constant terror. What if they send me to a detention camp?” he said. “I cannot bear to think about being separated from my children and grandchildren at this age, especially when all my ancestors have been buried in India.”

blocks.caption: BJP supporters celebrate during vote counting at state elections in West Bengal in May 2026. Photograph: Dibyangshu Sarkar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Critics say the problems began in 2023, when the Modi government changed the process for appointing the three-body election commission, giving majority control to the government for the first time. Within a matter of months, the Modi-led panel had appointed Kumar as the election commissioner in spite of opposition objections.
after newsletter promotion

“For decades, the election commission was one of our more credible, independent bodies, but now that has been eroded,” said Ronojoy Sen, a senior fellow at the South Asian Studies Programme, National University of Singapore.

By the following year, the new election commission body had begun SIR, starting in Bihar, where it immediately raised concerns among human rights groups after more than 6 million names were removed. Not long after the revisions, the BJP won a landslide victory in the Bihar state elections.

Despite concerns over SIR rumbling on for months, it did not spark national protests until the Indian Express newspaper last month revealed that two members of the election commission had raised 14 objections to how voters were being excluded from the rolls, but they were unilaterally overruled by Kumar.

“India has always been a flawed democracy but at least citizens felt they had the right to vote and that elections were regular and fair,” said Sen. “SIR has taken away that right. From how it has been conducted, it’s difficult to see how the motive was anything other than to enhance the election prospects of the BJP.”

Three former election commissioners have openly criticised SIR as a “hostile exercise” that has undermined the sanctity of the country’s electoral rolls by focusing on the exclusion – rather than inclusion – of voters. OP Rawat, a former chief election commissioner, described changes to the voter registration form as “wrong and illegal”.

Ashok Lavasa, who was an election commissioner between 2018 and 2020, called for the SIR to be scrapped. “An unfair procedure has been imposed on millions of people in the country, and you have the judiciary which has validated that,” he said last month. “How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?”

None have been more vehement in their opposition than SY Qureshi, who was chief election commissioner between 2010 and 2012. “This is a national harassment exercise designed to throw Muslims off the electoral roll,” he claimed. “The only way to restore the credibility of India’s elections is to restore those deleted voters.”

The BJP has denied any political involvement or motive in the SIR process, accusing the opposition Congress party of “jealousy” over its recent electoral victories and saying any deleted voters can simply re-enrol. The BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi said the allegations were “disinformation” and part of an opposition campaign “being orchestrated to create an atmosphere of division and anarchy”.

Nonetheless, the election commission has appeared to accept some flaws in the process. Late last week, it belatedly put a cap on the number of voter deletion forms – which allow people to submit objections on behalf of others – after incidents in which people submitted thousands of forms targeting legitimate Muslim voters.
Public anger, meanwhile, has continued to build. In Delhi, where the SIR exercise left millions of people off the draft list, protests are expected to continue this week.

A Delhi resident for 30 years, Prashant Tandon, 60, said he could not believe it when a notice came to his door, questioning his life as a voter. “If someone doubts my citizenship, they should produce evidence against me,” he said furiously, adding that he would be protesting alongside the young people. “I should not have to prove that I am an Indian citizen.”
Additional reporting Aakash Hassan

articles.title: Russia detains Japanese journalist, accusing him of alleged spying
articles.summary:
FSB security agency said reporter was arrested on island of Sakhalin, alleging he was collecting information about Russia’s defences

Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist on the far east…

blocks.text: Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist on the far east island of Sakhalin and accused him of espionage, Moscow said on Tuesday.

Russia regards Japan as an “unfriendly” country because it has joined western sanctions over its war ⁠in Ukraine. Russia has arrested several citizens of “unfriendly” countries in recent years, accusing them of working for western intelligence services.

Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova identified the reporter as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, saying Imai was accredited with the ministry but was accused of “conducting espionage activities on Russian territory”.
Japan’s embassy in Moscow told news agency Kyodo that the government was trying to ascertain the journalist’s reported detention.

Russia’s FSB security agency said a Japanese national, who it did not name, was arrested on Sakhalin and alleged he had worked for Japanese intelligence to collect information about Russia’s defences.

The FSB published a video showing masked officers storming a hotel room, pushing a man to the floor and handcuffing him. The man was flown to Moscow, where a court ordered he be held in pre-trial detention. It did not say when the arrest or court hearing occurred. The charges carry up to 20 years in prison.

Moscow and Tokyo have been locked in a territorial dispute for decades over the status of a string of islands in the Pacific Ocean, off the north-east coast of Japan and to the south-west of Russia’s Sakhalin region.
The FSB said it had “opened a criminal case against the Japanese national”, and that he had been placed in pre-trial detention, Russian news agencies reported, citing the agency.
Russian media reported he would remain in custody until 12 December.

“Attempts by Tokyo to use its correspondents in Russia … to gather information aimed at undermining the security of our state is regrettable,” Zakharova said, alleging this was “not an isolated case”.
The Kuril islands – which Japan calls the Northern Territories – have been under Russia’s control since the end of the second world war, when they were seized by the Soviet Union.

Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, visited one of the disputed islands in August, causing an ​uproar in Japan. Tokyo has ‌said it would continue ​implementing sanctions against ​Russia and supporting Ukraine.
In 2023, US journalist Evan Gershkovich was arrested on espionage charges, later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being released in a 2024 prisoner swap.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: What we know about the man who died falling from a Six Flags rollercoaster
articles.summary: Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died on Monday after police say he was ejected from a ride at a Six Flags amusement park in Georgia.

blocks.text: The Cobb County Police Department said the incident at the Six Flags Over Georgia park happened just before 16:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on Monday.
"Officers working at the park responded to an incident involving a male guest on a roller coaster," it said in a statement on Tuesday.
"Preliminary information gathered through witness and employee interview indicates Kariem was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction."

The ride involved has not been specified but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, and multiple witnesses have identified the ride as the one involved in the incident.
The office of the state's insurance and fire safety commissioner, which enforces amusement park safety rules in Georgia, is also conducting a review.
Officials have not held a news conference on the incident.

The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five.
The company said in a statement that it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident" and that "our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones".
Nick Mendenhall said he witnessed the fatal moments in disbelief, watching the man come out of his seat and then fall into another cart on the ride before falling to the ground.
"It was just super, super bizarre, traumatic. I mean, it took me a couple of seconds, I feel like, to process what was going on," he told the AP. "I cant believe that I just saw that."
He said his mind instantly went to the trauma of all of those impacted by what he witnessed, including the man's loved ones and everyone who was on the ride with him.

One witness told NBC affiliate WXIA that the incident was captured in souvenir photos that were automatically taken of the rollercoaster while it was in motion. The BBC has not been able to verify this statement.
Connor Thompson told the BBC's US partner CBS News that he was in line for the ride when everyone started "yelling, clearly distressed".

"Everyone was kind of confused at first, and then there was someone who was yelling, 'Call 911! Someone fell out!" he said. "At first it was almost like I didn't believe it because I thought that was like impossible for something like that to happen."
He said he saw the cart come into the hub where others were waiting in line and could see the restraint was unlatched.
Another witness, CiCi Nelson, told CNN she, too, was in line to ride the Goliath when the rollercoaster returned and she saw an empty seat with a loose safety bar and a female covered in blood.
Nelson described a scene of hysteria, adding that one man was "freaking out, saying someone fell off".
Brittany Landry, who believed she saw Kariem ejected from the rollercoaster, told Fox News she was in tears.
"I broke because we were just on there," she said.
Kariem's family said he was a father, passionate educator and had survived two bouts of cancer.
His family told WXIA that he had survived cancer twice - the last stint in 2018 - and was in a car crash with his 10-year-old daughter three weeks before his death.
He lived in the nearby city of Atlanta and worked for Wesley International Academy, a public charter school, for more than 12 years as an IT manager, technology teacher and robotics coach.
"Mr. Kariem was deeply loved and respected, and his absence will be felt throughout our school community," the school said in a statement posted to its Facebook account.
"His love for Wesley, dedication to our students, and commitment to our school community were evident in everything he did."

Outside of work, Kariem enjoyed creating products with his laser engraver and 3D printers, as well as cooking, watching anime and spending time with family and friends, according to his profile on the school's website.
The death at Six Flags Over Georgia is at least the seventh there, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tracks amusement park accidents and represents victims.

According to the firm, this includes two people who had medical emergencies, two who were in restricted areas when they were struck by a ride, two who died in car-related accidents and one who died months after using the park's pool.
Six Flags operates 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico.

In the last 15 years, two deaths caused by falling from the park's rollercoasters led to lawsuits and settlements. One in 2011 involved an Iraq War veteran who was ejected from a ride in New York and hit his head on the car. In the other, in 2013, a woman slipped from her restraints on a rollercoaster in Texas and fell 75 feet.
In September, the Six Flags Magic Mountain park in California announced it was closing its X2 rollercoaster after more 100 people alleged that they had suffered brain injuries from the ride.
With additional reporting by Brandon Drenon

articles.title: Graduate student accused of poisoning colleague and trying to flee to China arrested at LAX
articles.summary:
Microbiologist Aili Wang, 32, poisoned tea of colleague in Wyoming who had pending patents, prosecutors allege

A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on…

blocks.text: A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she did not get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her.

Aili Wang, 32, was arrested 6 October at Los Angeles international airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China. With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment – research similar to work she had done in China.

Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles. She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim’s wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.
US officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities.
The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations left him reeling. He was uncertain if the victim will fully recover.

“It’s been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your students’ lives is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that,” Gomelsky told the Associated Press. “That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career.”
Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.

The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as “KT”, began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water. The victim and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie.

Wang allegedly was recorded 27 September going through the alleged victim’s desk. On 1 October, she was recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer’s affidavit said.
Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.
The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said.
He also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said. When he washed the coffee maker, Gomelsky said, the taste would go away.
Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.
Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine.
It’s not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany county circuit court judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors’ request and raised bond to $1.5m cash-only.
Wang allegedly asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer, police said.

articles.title: Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines
articles.summary: Four years after the attacks, Serhii K will appear in court accused of a plot to destroy Russia's gas pipelines to Germany.

blocks.text: Four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history, a Ukrainian man goes on trial in Hamburg on Wednesday accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany.
Serhii K, as he is identified by German prosecutors, is accused of plotting with other Ukrainian military personnel to destroy the pipelines and stop Russia financing its war with gas revenue.
The case is highly sensitive in Germany, seen as one of Ukraine's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, seven months before the attacks took place.
Serhii K, extradited to Germany last year, will become the first suspect to go on trial for the blasts.
He denies the charges, as does a second suspect who is fighting extradition from Croatia.

In the months after explosives destroyed three of the four gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea off the island of Bornholm on 26 September 2022, Western suspicion looked towards Moscow without directly apportioning blame.

Russia had already shut off the flow of gas to Germany in Nord Stream 1 weeks before the attack, and Nord Stream 2 had never been turned on. Berlin had frozen the multi-billion dollar project shortly before the invasion and there were reports of suspicious Russian naval movements before the blasts.
The case has highlighted differences of opinion on the trial in Kyiv and Berlin.

Oleksandr Merezhko, who chairs the Foreign Affairs Committee in the Ukrainian parliament, points out that the blasts took place during a time of war with Russia and "Nord Stream 2 was nothing but a tool used by Russia in order to get prepared for the war".
He told the BBC they had no confirmation of the German account: "It's one of the versions."
However, Stefan Meister, of the German Council on Foreign Relations, says successive chancellors in Berlin have done their best to remove the politics from the case.

"They tried to make not a big story out of it, not to give it too much attention, to give it to the institutions, to the judiciary that they will deal with it. This is not a political case. So they tried to depoliticise it," he explained.

In August 2025, Serhii K was arrested after checking into a hotel near the Italian Adriatic resort of Rimini, by police acting under a European arrest warrant issued by federal prosecutors in Germany.
After several weeks of court battles fighting extradition, Serhii K - identified in court documents as Serhii Kuznetsov - was transferred to Germany late last year.
German prosecutors allege that in 2022 he was a serving officer in the Ukrainian army, external, and he had led a group of professional divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert.
While his legal fight was going on in Italy, another Ukrainian man called Volodymyr Zhuravlov successfully challenged Germany's extradition bid in a Polish court.

In a ruling very different from Italy's Supreme Court, the Polish judge ordered Zhuravlov's release in October 2025, stating that the attack on the pipelines was not unlawful, and if Ukraine had organised an armed mission it was "justified, rational and just".
Although he was released by the court in Warsaw, he was arrested last August in Croatia on suspicion of being a suspect who "participated in the dives necessary" for the sabotage.
Last month, Croatia approved his extradition, although it is not clear when that will happen, and if his case could become part of the Hamburg trial.

Despite the difficult nature of the case for Kyiv and Berlin, Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko does not believe it will spoil relations as "it's in the best national interests of Germany to continue to support us".

articles.title: Pictured: Winning entries for Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026
articles.summary: Striking images including an urban coyote and an elephant carrying a dead calf are among this year's winners.

blocks.text: An emotional scene of an elephant carrying a deceased calf has earned Italian photographer Federico Veronesi the title of Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026.
While tracking elephants in Namibia's Huab River Valley, Veronesi spotted an unusual trail of drag marks across the sand of a dry riverbed.
Following the tracks, he came across a female elephant carrying a dead calf, its leg wedged between her tusk and trunk.
Initially, Veronesi assumed the elephant was the calf's mother. But after sharing his photographs with an elephant research project working in the area, he learned that this wasn't certain.
Researchers recognised the elephant as a female who had lost a calf several years earlier and said she had previously picked up dead calves belonging to other females.

For Veronesi, the encounter was deeply significant. "Of all the 20 years I've done photographing animals, this is the most heart-wrecking and fascinating and dramatic," he said, describing it as "revealing of the depth and complexity of the emotions, the feelings of the animals."

He hopes the image will encourage people to look beyond animals' physical appearance and recognise them as individuals with their own relationships, memories and emotions. "It's a small window that opens just a crack into the complexity of their world," he said.
The competition's annual exhibition, external opens at the Natural History Museum on Friday 16 October 2026. Keep scrolling to see more award-winning images.

articles.title: 'I'd talk to the TV': The paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely
articles.summary: As loneliness grows in China, a new industry is emerging to provide companionship and support.

blocks.text: 'I'd talk to the TV': The paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely
Watch: Why the lonely in China are hiring 'temporary children'
"The biggest difficulty really was the loneliness. Sometimes, if I wanted to talk to someone I'd talk to the TV."
Yang, 91, lives on the outskirts of China's bustling capital Beijing. Following the death of her husband, she was so lonely that she says she even considered the possibility of voluntary euthanasia.
"I asked my son about it but he told me it was banned. I told him that if it ever becomes legal I want to do it - I didn't want to live any longer."
Suffering glaucoma, with failing eyesight, she was unable to even do basic things like adjust the controls on her air conditioner.

Cases such as Yang's have become increasingly common in Chinese cities which Associate Professor Teresa Kuan, from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, says is "exacerbated by the structure of society and the modes by which people interact".

There are many causes of isolation in China. Most of it happens when rural migrants pursue economic opportunities, leaving behind close-knit support networks for urban centres where loneliness and uncertainty can be difficult to overcome, or when graduates uproot themselves chasing employment on the other side of the country.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Suffering from glaucoma and failing eyesight, 91-year-old Yang found simple tasks and daily life increasingly difficult on her own.

blocks.text: Suffering from glaucoma and failing eyesight, 91-year-old Yang found simple tasks and daily life increasingly difficult on her own.
But now a growing "loneliness industry" has emerged to try to fill these gaps in people's lives.

Yang says her life has been transformed by one of these services - Wang Yingwei and his electric scooter delivery team - who started coming over twice a day with hot meals but whose help extends far beyond that.
"We see ourselves as community children," Yingwei told the BBC. "It means putting yourself in the shoes of older people and carefully considering their needs.

"For example, they may be drinking tap water which can be cloudy and contain a lot of lime. I can fix this problem with a filtered water tank. Such a small thing can make them much happier. Maybe they can't shower because their equipment is broken. I'll buy a part, replace it and their shower is fine."
"The elderly treat us like their children, and we treat them like our own parents," he added.
Yingwei's services cost less than half the price of employing a caregiver.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Wang Yingwei and his small delivery team offer more than just meals, bringing human connection to elderly residents.

blocks.text: Wang Yingwei and his small delivery team offer more than just meals, bringing human connection to elderly residents.

The former mobile phone salesman says he started his company to help seniors remain at home without having to move into retirement facilities. He was inspired to do this after his own father-in-law, who had developed Alzheimer's, had to go into a nursing home. Yingwei said he felt that the conditions there were so sub-standard he wanted to make sure others could stay out of institutions like this for as long as possible.
His small business currently employs four people but he says there is a possibility he will expand as demand grows.

There is still a shortage of solid data on the size of this sector – which operators say has exploded in recent years – but securities company Sinolink valued it at around $7.4 billion in 2025. And this is only expected to grow given the trajectory of modern lifestyles.
Zheng Ruizhi, another client of Yingwei's who lives in Beijing's northern outskirts, welcomed him at the door with a big smile.
"After retiring, I don't have much opportunity to hang out with others," the 75-year-old, whose son lives two hours away from her, told the BBC.
She was recovering from a recent injury which she said was making everyday tasks more difficult.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zheng Ruizhi, 75, shares a lighthearted moment with Wang Yingwei during a home visit.

blocks.text: Zheng Ruizhi, 75, shares a lighthearted moment with Wang Yingwei during a home visit.
But the arrival of Yingwei – who she calls her "dear boy" – lightened her mood.

"I call you 'dear boy' because I am so fond of you. I genuinely like you from the bottom of my heart. I also admire and trust you. When you help me out, I don't have a single worry or fear," she told him.
Yet the services offered by those in this sector are not limited to home visits.

Twenty-three-year-old Liu Yanyan, for instance, works as a "medical escort". She acts as a friendly face taking clients to see the doctor, or picking up their test results or medication from city hospitals, which can be intimidatingly large and bureaucratic.

"Some of my customers are people in their 20s who came to Beijing to build a career. They might not have friends here or feel awkward asking colleagues to accompany them because of the concept of social reciprocity in Chinese culture," she said. "If I accompanied you to a doctor's appointment for free, you might feel obligated to buy me a meal or a movie ticket afterwards."
She said that, because of this, there are many people in modern Chinese society who tend to keep to themselves.
"So, they hire someone like me to accompany them to the hospital. If they had to go alone, they could feel scared or anxious."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Liu Yanyan, a 23-year-old medical escort, helps clients navigate complex city hospitals.

blocks.text: Liu Yanyan, a 23-year-old medical escort, helps clients navigate complex city hospitals.
At the core of many businesses catering to loneliness in China is a simple offering: human connection.
Teresa Kuan said that some people prefer the option of pouring their hearts out to a complete stranger for a fee.

"If there is a companion you have paid for, the relationship is not exactly equal. It is a service relationship, so you don't have to deal with the unpredictability of a standard relationship. The thing about friendship is that it can be unpredictable. You don't know when someone might disappoint you. But, in a service relationship, you have a better idea of what to expect."
Wang Zhoutao runs a hiking business to help people who want to climb China's famous mountain Huangshan in Anhui Province.
"We provide emotional support, like cheering them up, taking their photo or telling jokes. It's really a service based on companionship," he said.
The former soldier added that he normally hikes up the mountain with clients 10 to 15 days a month. When fully booked, this could be as many as 30 times a month.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mountain escort Wang Zhoutao guides a client up the steep steps of Mount Huangshan.

blocks.text: Mountain escort Wang Zhoutao guides a client up the steep steps of Mount Huangshan.
He gave an example of a young woman he once accompanied who felt ostracised at work. "She felt useless and wanted to prove something to herself," he said.

"We started climbing but it was a tough trek as the weather was really hot and we were sweating a lot. There were moments she wanted to give up but I told her, 'If you quit now and can't get over this mountain how will you handle anything else in life?'. I kept encouraging her."
After they made it all the way he said she sent him a long message of thanks describing her inner journey and expressing her gratitude.

"The pace of life is just too fast these days. People face pressure from work, relationships and family expectations," he said. "I think my clients are mostly people who feel a void in their relationships or have suffered a setback."
Human connection is a necessity but, in a society grappling with loneliness across generations, it has now also become a commodity.
Back in her little Beijing flat, Yang is feeling more comfortable now that Yingwei has sorted out her problem of making the air conditioner work properly.
"It's good to have someone around when you need it, someone you can share your innermost thoughts with," she said.
"I did struggle with loneliness but that's been resolved now. I'm quite happy.
"I can't lose Yingwei and the others. They've all got a good heart."

articles.title: Who's to blame for the toxic smog choking South East Asia?
articles.summary: Anger is mounting at the companies accused of burning land in Indonesia and the authorities who have failed to stop them.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Wildfires have been raging in Kalimantan, Indonesia for weeks
ByKoh Ewe
Reporting fromSingapore
As Indonesia battles its worst wildfire season in a decade, a toxic smog is choking millions of residents in the region.
The air on the islands of Kalimantan and Sumatra have turned an ominous amber, with air quality recorded at hazardous levels.

The smog - also known as the haze - has also drifted beyond Indonesia's borders to neighbouring countries, raising public health concerns. It has obscured Singapore's skyline and forced some schools to close in Malaysia.
Now, anger is mounting at the companies accused of burning farmland - as well as the authorities who have struggled to stop them.
The annual dry season wildfires have been especially intense this year because of an unusually strong El Niño - a natural climate phenomenon which changes weather patterns around the world.
According to independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas, 1,043,377 wildfire hotspots have been recorded in Indonesia, burning a total of 900,000 hectares of land.
Slash and burn
Many of these fires in Indonesia's forests and peatlands are caused by the razing of vegetation to clear land - a practice known as "slash and burn".
This is an agricultural method that has traditionally been employed by farmers in Indonesia to create nutrient-rich soil for new crops.

But today, many of these fires are associated with commercial farming and are taking place on a much larger scale - and are harder to control. Activists and government investigations have repeatedly accused some companies of using fire as a cheap way to clear large swathes of land.
While slash-and-burn farming is illegal in Indonesia, enforcement of a ban has long proven tricky.
But persistent haze this year has prompted Indonesian authorities to step up efforts to punish offenders.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has called for tougher sanctions against slash-and-burn farming, describing the practice as "ecological terrorism".

Last month, Indonesian authorities announced they had suspended the operating licences of 26 companies linked to the wildfires and launched investigations into others. Cases involving criminal elements would be taken to court, officials vowed.
But it's not just Indonesian companies that have been embroiled in controversy amid the haze problem.
Watch: What makes fires in Indonesia so hard to extinguish?
A Greenpeace report published this month identified businesses based in Singapore and Malaysia which are linked to plots of land in Indonesia where wildfires are burning.

This includes First Resources, a Singapore-based palm oil company. Between August and September more than 30 haze source points were recorded on land managed by its two Indonesian subsidiaries, according to Greenpeace.

First Resources told the BBC in a statement that it maintained a "strict zero burning policy across all planting activities and implement robust fire prevention, monitoring and firefighting measures throughout our operations".
Greenpeace also named Malaysian plantation group Kuala Lumpur Kepong, whose subsidiary PT Menteng Jaya Sawit Perdana managed land in Indonesia where 19 haze source points were recorded.
Kuala Lumpur Kepong said in a statement that a "majority" of the fires originated from beyond its concession area and had all been extinguished.
"We do not condone or permit the use of open burning for land preparation or any other purpose across our operations," it said.
'When there is no smoke, we send oxygen'
It remains to be seen how effective governments can be in sanctioning offending companies.
In 2014, Singapore passed the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act which allows the government to take action against local and foreign firms found to be contributing to the haze.

The following year when Singapore saw a bad bout of haze, authorities issued summonses to several Indonesian companies thought to have cleared land by burning, in a bid to prosecute them under the new law.

But that drew sharp ire from Jakarta, which said the move harmed bilateral ties. And with Indonesia refusing to cooperate, Singapore authorities said they could not obtain information about the suspected companies.

Also in 2015, Indonesia's then-Vice-President Jusuf Kalla angered Singaporeans when he said that "for 11 months, they enjoyed nice air from Indonesia and they never thanked us... they have suffered because of the haze for one month and they get upset".

Similar tensions surfaced again last weekend when Syahganda Nainggolan, who leads Indonesia's government communications agency, said the raging wildfires were beyond human control and added that the oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".
"When there is no smoke, we send oxygen," he added, in a video that has been widely circulated on social media, triggering criticism and ridicule from Malaysians and Singaporeans.
Watch: Toxic smog makes thousands sick as Indonesia wildfires rage
But Indonesia has in the past also apologised to its neighbours for causing the haze.
This year, Indonesian officials have thanked Singapore and Malaysia for offering to help tackle the wildfires - though it has not officially requested international support.
In Indonesia, there have been efforts by civil society to force the government to take action.

In Pontianak in the West Kalimantan province, several groups have filed a class action lawsuit against the Indonesian government and Prabowo, accusing them of "gross negligence" over recurrent toxic haze.
They want the government to declare the haze a national disaster, which would allow for recovery measures such as the coverage of healthcare costs.
A similar case was filed last year in South Sumatra, but it was dismissed.
Meanwhile, on the ground in Kalimantan and Sumatra, air pollution levels have remained at dangerous levels for weeks.
There are many who have no choice but to brave the toxic smog every day.

"I'm short of breath and have a headache breathing air now. But I still have to work," Imrayedi, a 63-year-old motorcycle taxi driver in Pekanbaru city, on Sumatra island, told BBC Indonesian last week.
"The government must also think about the common people like us. Please take action to find a solution so that this haze problem can be resolved immediately."
