items: 13m agoWelcome

blocks.caption: Ben Doherty

blocks.text: Ben Doherty
The Josh Frydenberg book-promotion/comeback-to-politics tour continues.
The former treasurer, and ousted member for Kooyong, appeared on 7:30 last night, again raising the possibility of his return to frontline politics.
His memoir, A Grateful Son, is the Trojan Horse that legitimises questions like: “Do you think you’d make a good prime minister?”

“Look, I haven’t closed the door to reentering politics,” Frydenberg reiterated. “That would involve running for a seat, winning it, joining the party room and then proceeding after that. So there are a lot of steps.”
He told host Sarah Ferguson that “if I was to run, it would be at the next election”, but insisted “it’s not a decision that I have taken”.
Full marks for persistence, Ferguson tried again: “Do you have what it takes to lead the country?”

Frydenberg: “Look, I think it’s important to know what you believe in, and I certainly do, to have policy ideas that can take the country in the right direction, and to be consistent with the philosophy and the values of our great party, and that’s what I articulate in the book.”

blocks.caption: Sarah Basford Canales

blocks.text: Sarah Basford Canales

Gas companies would be forced to set aside 20% of exports for Australian use under new legislation for a national gas reservation scheme to be introduced, with Labor committing to more transparency and tighter rules to prevent the system from being gamed.
The resources minister, Madeleine King, will introduce the amended bills that will give the Australian Energy Regulator the power to force companies to meet a target of 110% of demand each year.
It will also limit ministerial discretion and replace the Turnbull-era domestic gas security mechanism.

In a speech to be delivered at the National Press Club King will say a successful energy transition for the country will rely on a “guaranteed supply of affordable gas” for households, renewable energies and the processing of critical minerals and rare earths.
King will also say Australia must continue exporting traditional commodities, including gas and coal.

double quotation markNo two countries will follow exactly the same pathway to reducing emissions. What remains important is the commitment to the goal and a peaceful and inclusive journey toward it, so that we can minimise the damage caused by climate change, while making sure our communities have the energy they need.
Mark Dreyfus has fired off a warning to social media platforms about the livestream of US military execution planned for December.
The former attorney, who is now the special envoy for international human rights, said Australia held longstanding opposition to the death penalty and had raised it with the United States.

double quotation markAustralia opposes the death penalty in all circumstances, for all people ... the proposed livestreaming of an execution is deeply distressing. Platforms have a responsibility to prevent this disturbing content from being shown to Australians.
Yesterday, Anthony Albanese said he found the proposed streaming of a firing squad execution “completely abhorrent”, adding “we should do whatever we can to stop that occurring”.
The prime minister told ABC social media platforms risked harming their reputation for allowing streams of the execution but the government was limited in shutting them down.
Albanese said the government was receiving advice on its options. He said:
double quotation markIf there is something, anything we can do, we will do. I assure you of that.

blocks.caption: Tom McIlroy

blocks.text: Tom McIlroy
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, has urged progressives not to disregard voters that are attracted to One Nation’s message in the Bernie Fraser oration at the Shine Dome in Canberra last night.
Chalmers said Pauline Hanson would be a disaster in government, calling One Nation “inexperienced, incompetent and incapable of managing the economy or our international reputation”.
But the treasurer said a significant number of Australians see value in the One Nation-aligned message of returning to the “good old days”.
double quotation markOur role as progressive people is not to scold those who see appeal in that message. It’s not to mock them, dare I say cancel them, or talk down to them.
He said the government should instead genuinely acknowledge the pressures people are under and deliver measures to make people’s lives better.

double quotation markThe far right strategy is to divide people and it’s working; their goal is to talk down our economy so that their endless negativity becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. Their core message is often clear and sometimes very appealing: let’s just go back to a more nostalgic version of the world we remember. We have all the facts to push back on this, but facts don’t beat feelings. Feelings are as real as facts.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Krishani Dhanji with the main action.

articles.title: Ukraine allies in Poland after Starlink sabotage, Trump diesel deal
articles.summary: Germany's Johann Wadephul said hybrid plots like the Starlink fire showed Europe was "in Russia's crosshairs." The UK's Ed Miliband said Trump's Russian diesel deal led to a "very difficult few days"…

image.caption: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said sanctions should continue being imposed on Russia's economy as attacks on Ukraine persistImage: Jörg Blank/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The foreign ministers of Germany, Norway, Poland and the UK spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday.

This came as investigators in Germany were chasing down suspects for a fire at a Starlink station in Poland, and as Ukraine's European allies scrambled to deal with US President Donald Trump's latest lurch into Vladimir Putin's lap.
What did the ministers say about Russian diesel and Ukraine?

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul bemoaned the US decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal to supply the US — seemingly struck as Trump panics about fuel prices with the Iran war still unresolved and a month to go until midterm elections.
"I would say this is not the time to lower the sanctions regime but to strengthen this," Wadephul said, noting the new package of EU sanctions imposed on Monday.
"We are keeping our course," he said, adding that Europe was asking the authorities in Washington to do the same.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband arguably found even clearer words.
"Within the bounds of diplomacy we should acknowledge that it's been a very difficult few days," Miliband said in the Polish capital that's just a few hours' drive from Ukraine's western border.

blocks.caption: Germany's Johann Wadephul, Poland's Radoslaw Sikorski, Norway's Espen Barth Eide and the UK's Ed Miliband shared a stage at the Warsaw Security Forum on TuesdayImage: Dominik Butzmann/photothek.de/picture alliance

blocks.text: Poland's Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, meanwhile, said he was counting on "our MAGA president" — a reference to Andrzej Duda of the rival PiS party whom Trump has often praised — to use his "friendship" with Trump to do two things.

"Number one: to secure a permanent US base in Poland. And, number two: to explain to him that Putin is the aggressor, and Zelenskyy is the victim of aggression, and you end the war by convincing the aggressor to limit his level of ambition, not by asking the victim to capitulate," Sikorski said.
Norway's Espen Barth Eide said it was important to focus on the actions of the last four years, also welcoming Monday's latest round of Russian sanctions.

"I feel that what we've done over the last years ... all of this is a very strong signal that Europe, together with Canada and — on most good days — also with the US, we are sending a very clear message to Putin," Eide said.

Facing criticism at home as well, Trump on Tuesday said that the US was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. He also said that other countries would be buying Russian diesel as part of the deal he announced, without being deemed to breach US sanctions, rather than the US buying it itself. This contradicted or possibly corrected his earlier statements.

blocks.caption: The first two Starlink arrests took place in the small German town of Nürtingen in the southwest, far from Poland's bordersImage: Enrique Kaczor/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Wadephul: Starlink sabotage shows Europe 'in the crosshairs' of Russia
Wadephul also told reporters during his visit that he had spoken with his opposite number Sikorski about the investigations into a fire at a Starlink station in Poland last month.

Two people with Turkish citizenship were arrested in Germany in the southwestern town of Nürtingen, not far from Stuttgart, on Monday. Based on comments from Polish officials, they are suspected of connections with organized criminality but are thought to have been working on behalf of Russia.
Wadephul said that this and other hybrid incidents across the continent showed that "we are in Russia's crosshairs."
The satellite-based Starlink internet service is used extensively by Ukraine's military and so the fire was thought to be targeted accessibility across the border in the warzone.
"We're being attacked and it's not just happening in Ukraine but all across Europe," he said. "That means we must strengthen our cooperation."
But he also said that the arrests in Germany, which will likely lead to an exatradition process, showed how the security systems were working — both at the policing and intelligence-gathering levels.
He said he did not believe Russia would succeed in "dividing us" with such campaigns, saying that instead he expected they would galvanize European allies.
A private Polish broadcaster meanwhile reported two further arrests in Germany on Tuesday, although German authorities did not immediately comment on them.

blocks.caption: Miliband and Sikorski, who spent many of his younger years in the UK, also held a joint press conference in Warsaw on TuesdayImage: Neil Milton/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Miliband praises Zelenskyy, but says 'let us take seriously' energy ceasefire idea

UK Foreign Secretary Miliband praised Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for showing "extraordinary leadership ... in the most difficult of circumstances" since Putin's 2022 full-scale invasion, shortly after Trump's call — mirroring Russian messaging — for presidential elections in war-torn Ukraine.

However, Miliband also said the notion of an "energy ceasefire" raised by Trump — seemingly unilaterally — was nevertheless worthy of consideration given the attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and the onset of winter.
"So let us take up this idea of the full energy ceasefire and let us seek with President Trump to hold Putin to this full energy ceasefire, because that is what we need," Miliband said.
Miliband noted how Zelenskyy had expressed a willingness in theory, even if Russia was yet to do so.
Wadephul added that, if possible, any such efforts to broker a partial ceasefire should also seek to incoporate grain exports and shipments in the Black Sea, particuarly to North Africa.

"This is still necessary. And let us please not forget this and urge Russia also to be ready to enlarge the ceasefire, not only for the energy sector but also for the Black Sea. Because this is needed to stop a lot of people in North Africa from falling into hunger," he said.
Trump announces 'energy ceasefire' in Ukraine war

articles.title: Ukraine and the US: What's next after Trump’s diesel deal with Russia?
articles.summary: Donald Trump plans to allow the purchase of Russian diesel, drawing criticism at home and abroad. What is behind the US president’s decision and what should Ukraine do next? DW spoke with experts.

image.caption: Gas prices are on the rise in the USImage: Patrick T. Fallon/AFP

blocks.text: The diesel deal between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin has sparked anger in Ukraine. Under the agreement, Moscow is allowed to supply Russian diesel fuel to global markets. The US news website Axios reported the move came in response to Kyiv's failure to comply with Washington's demands to stop attacks on oil refineries in Russia.
Trump also declared that it was time "for Ukraine to get a new president."
The agreement to sell diesel was announced while talks between Ukrainian, US and European representatives were taking place in Miami.

"I think our team is simply being used as a cover. That is definitely not fair," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists shortly afterwards, describing Trump's decision as "a weak decision by strong partners."
From the Oval Office to Miami
This is hardly Kyiv's first crisis in its relationship with the Trump administration. In February 2025, Trump told Zelenskyy in the Oval Office "you don’t have the cards."

The White House confrontation was followed by a suspension of weapons deliveries and intelligence-sharing agreements. According to media reports, US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened to suspend intelligence sharing during the talks in Miami, too, citing Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries as the reason. US officials have denied the reports.

blocks.caption: Memories are rekindled of the February 2025 spat between Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Donald Trump and JD VanceImage: Jim Lo Scalzo/UPI Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: The current tension recalls the dispute in the White House at the time, says Mykhailo Honchar of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies "Strategy XXI" in an interview with DW. However, he says there is no reason for Ukrainians to panic.

"Last year, too, there were threats and suspensions of intelligence sharing, as well as disruptions in weapons supplies," he said. "Then the Americans realized how much this was hurting them, too, and reluctantly resumed everything."
Is Trump looking for a 'scapegoat?'

All the experts interviewed by DW see a connection between Trump's threats toward Ukraine and the US midterm elections on November 3. In the midterms, all seats in the House of Representatives and roughly one third of Senate seats are up for election.
Ivan Us of the National Institute for Strategic Studies in Kyiv expects a crushing defeat for the Republicans. He says the main reason will be high fuel prices.

"Donald Trump wants desperately to distract attention from the fact that high prices are linked to his war with Iran and the problems in the Strait of Hormuz. He needs a scapegoat for this. And he has decided that Ukraine will be it," the expert said.
Mykhailo Honchar sees Russia as the main beneficiary of Trump's deal with Putin: "This whole diesel deal looks like a disguised request from Putin to Trump to exert influence on Ukraine."

Honchar also links the agreement to a possible sale of the foreign assets of Russian oil company Lukoil. According to The New York Times, potential buyers of these assets include investors with ties to Trump.
Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again?
How can the crisis be resolved?
Oleksandr Kraiev of the Ukrainian think tank Ukrainian Prism warns against taking drastic action.

"Slamming the door in anger will certainly not help us. In that case, security assistance and intelligence sharing will be off the table. We cannot afford that. It may be difficult, and sometimes even repulsive, but we have to maintain contact with the Americans," the expert said.

At the same time, Ukraine could work with Germany, Denmark, the United Kingdom and France to make deliveries of Russian diesel fuel "simply unrealistic." After all, the tankers would have to pass through these countries' territorial waters on their way to the United States, and the partners have already said they would not allow this.
Ivan Us advises against reading too much into the harsh rhetoric.
"You can say whatever you want in public, as long as you carry on as before," he said of the possible relationship between Kyiv and Washington.

Ukrainian diplomats should work with US Republicans and the MAGA movement. Trump's agreement with Putin is already being criticized in those circles, with some raising concerns that Russia could use the proceeds from the diesel trade to support Iran.

Us also does not rule out a legal challenge to Trump's decision. Republican Senator Tom Tillis told NBC that the president was likely violating a 2022 law prohibiting imports of Russian oil and other energy products.
Ivan Us considers US threats to cut Ukraine off from intelligence or weapons to be little more than "fearmongering" ahead of the elections.
"The US makes such statements not because it intends to take action, but to make the markets believe that it is about to exert pressure and thereby drive prices down," Us said.
What will change after November 3?

The three experts agree that Kyiv should ride out the situation until after the US midterm elections on November 3. Oleksandr Kraiev says he is sure that Trump may back down on this issue after the elections, since abandoning Ukraine would mean showing weakness toward China.

Mykhailo Honchar points out that Trump's deal with Putin is already being criticized by Republicans in both the Senate and the House of Representatives. In addition, Republican Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick has introduced a bipartisan bill named after former US President Ronald Reagan that would block purchases of Russian oil.

"Despite all the threats, and perhaps even some attempts to impose temporary measures against Kyiv, it is unlikely that Trump will go any further. The situation should not be portrayed in apocalyptic terms," Honchar said.
He added that Trump's pressure was also bringing Ukraine and its European partners closer together.
This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

articles.title: California coastal homes battered and bruised after weekend of intense waves and flooding
articles.summary:
Boardwalk destroyed in Long Beach and homes damaged, while Baja California in Mexico and Las Vegas also affected

Southern California coastal communities are picking up the pieces after a…

blocks.text: Southern California coastal communities are picking up the pieces after a weekend of extreme weather brought flooding that overtook city streets and intense waves battered beachside homes.

The remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel hit Mexico’s Baja California over the weekend as well as southern California and Las Vegas. While meteorologists noted that Rachel weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it approached California, it still left a trail of destruction.
Footage showed massive waves crashing into Long Beach homes, destroying a boardwalk and forcing residents to flee. The damage to homes was significant, leaving some at risk of collapse.

At least nine have been deemed unsafe to enter, the Long Beach Post reported, meaning displaced residents cannot return to retrieve personal items. The storm has cost the city more than $1m from its emergency reserves, according to the outlet.

blocks.caption: Waves from tropical storm Rachel destroy beachfront houses - loop

blocks.text: Further south, the city of Newport Beach declared a local emergency and briefly closed piers to “protect public safety”, citing “higher-than-normal surf” that inundated streets.
By Monday, cleanup work was under way and Newport Beach had reopened the piers, but officials advised residents to exercise caution near the water.

In Las Vegas, a raging torrent of water rushed over a street near the strip, and the city tied an all-time daily rainfall record for October with 1.08in (2.74cm) of rain into Sunday morning, according to the US National Weather Service.

The extreme weather comes as El Niño is supercharging the Pacific, leading to large and long-lasting storms. The last five hurricanes in the Pacific all reached major status and saw with winds of at least 111mph (178.6 km/h), and one set a record for time spent at category 5.
Colorado State University researcher Phil Klotzbach, who forecasts and studies storm activity, told the Associated Press that the last month has been “berserk”.
“This year, just everything that forms is just lasting a long time and getting really powerful,” he said.

blocks.caption: Waves crash into homes and a sea wall in Long Beach. Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty Images

blocks.text: California is bracing for a challenging winter with severe storms thanks to an exceptionally strong El Niño. Models from the the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) show a high chance this could be a historic El Niño and deliver rainy wet weather, landslides and destructive high tides.

The state is one of the places expected to be significantly affected by the climate pattern, although the effects are expected to be seen worldwide, with temperature spikes and rising global food prices.
Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Saudi Arabia strikes strategic oil depots near Yemen capital
articles.summary:
Civilians warned to evacuate outskirts of Sana’a ahead of biggest attack so far on Houthi energy infrastructure

Saudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the…

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital Sana’a, in a fresh escalation of the conflict between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi forces.

Before the attack on Tuesday, a Saudi spokesperson warned civilians to leave the target area, in an apparent attempt to strike fear into the local population ahead of the biggest attack so far on Houthi energy infrastructure.

The Central Sabaha Station oil depot on the western side of the city contains large tanks that often holds substantial quantities of fuel derivatives, although the Yemeni Oil Company said its storage facilities were empty at the time of the attack.

Houthi oil depots at the Ras Isa port in Hodeidah, the subject of Israeli attacks in 2024, were also struck in 10 waves of attacks apparently aimed to immobilise the Houthi army as it continues its push South including towards the city of Taiz.
Earlier the Saudis also struck what they believe to be a Houthi leadership hide-out in Bani Mu’in area in the Razih border district, west of Saada governorate, northern Yemen.

The strike on the oil depot appeared to be the Saudi response to a Houthi attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday, that killed 13 and left 300 injured. The airport is closed until Saturday at the earliest, a blow to an economy that is trying to show its security makes the country a safe place to invest.

A Houthi spokesperson responded to the attack on its oil storage by warning “all employees and citizens present near any facility affiliated with Aramco Petroleum in Riyadh to evacuate it and stay away from it, as it is a legitimate target for our forces”.
The difference between the threats is that Saudi Arabia has complete air dominance over Yemen while the Houthis have to reply using drones and missiles which can be intercepted.

Baraa Shiban, a Yemen specialist at the defence thinktank Royal United Services Institute (Rusi), warned “Saudi Arabia is struggling to respond to the Houthi’s improved arms technology. Until relatively recently Houthi missiles and drones fell in desert areas or if they got through were intercepted. They have learned how to deploy drones that fly lower and are smaller, and are less easy to detect. They are cheap and it does not take many to get through to be effective”.
But the two sides’ dramatic threats to set ablaze the enemy energy infrastructure symbolised how the conflict is escalating rather than blowing itself out.

blocks.caption: A map released by the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition shows the targeted site of the Yemeni Oil Company and Al-Sabaha Central Station in Sana'a. Photograph: @CJFCS.

blocks.text: Donald Trump complained that the Houthis were “behaving very badly” and said he would “never forget” their attacks, which he suggested were an attempt to influence the US midterm elections next month. But he stopped short of announcing any new military action.

The latest phase of the conflict between the Saudis and the Houthis began last month after the rebels seized key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical waterway for the transportation of Gulf oil and other goods at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen.

This week, the Houthis have come closer to throttling the southern city of Taiz, drawing close enough to the city edges to fire rockets into residential areas. City leaders have made repeated appeals to the Yemeni government for military equipment while public health professionals warned of a shortage of medicines for patients in intensive care.
Government aligned forces sent reinforcement to the south west district of Al-Mudarabba in Lahij governorate as well as the mountain district of Al-Waz’iyya.

But anti-Houthi forces inside Yemen are not themselves united: a group known as the Southern Transitional Council has been taking a more prominent role in the fight against the Houthis – even though its main objective is to seccede from the country’s north.

On Tuesday, Aidarous al Zubaidi, the exiled STC leader, gave a rare address declaring “a popular mobilisation in defence of the south, and its national liberation project”, – including by repelling the invading Houthi militia.
Al Zubaidi, now based in Abu Dhabi, made clear he still supported a plan to eventually hold a referendum on the independence of South Yemen.

Zubaidi’s organisation remains banned in Yemen and he has been charged with treason, but there are incremental behind-the-scenes talks under way testing whether the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is prepared to legitimise the STC and even permit Zubaidi to return. Reinstatement of the STC would be seen as a betrayal by the current Yemen president, Rashad al-Alimi, but his usefulness to Saudi Arabia is reduced if he does have the same military forces at his disposal as Zubaidi.

articles.title: Inside Katie Zacharia's very brief White House briefing
articles.summary: The BBC's Sarah Smith was in the room and describes Zacharia's performance and the moment she broke news about Kimberly Guilfoyle being asked to resign.
